#4675. Pennsylvania is way ahead on NEVI charging – now comes another $37M

Pennsylvania is putting $37 million in federal NEVI funding toward what PennDOT says will be 515 new public EV charging ports across the Philadelphia region, including curbside chargers.

The awards cover Bucks, Chester, Delaware, Montgomery, and Philadelphia counties. PennDOT says the projects will expand public charging availability by 27% across the region and 53% in Philadelphia.

For drivers without a driveway, curbside charging gives them somewhere to plug in while parked near home.

It’s Electric PA received $2.93 million for 157 on-street Level 2 ports across 13 Philadelphia neighborhoods. Voltpost received funding for another 62 curbside ports across the four suburban counties.

Fast charging is getting funding, too. PositivEnergy received $7.2 million for 54 DC fast-charging ports at 11 Philadelphia Parking Authority lots. Tesla received two $392,000 awards for eight ports each at Royal Farms in Broomall and Wawa in Plymouth Meeting.

The money comes from the federal National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure (NEVI) program, created by the Biden administration’s Bipartisan Infrastructure Law. Pennsylvania’s five-year allocation is $171.5 million.

NEVI initially focused on fast charging along designated highway corridors. States can spend the money more broadly after the Federal Highway Administration certifies that their corridor charging requirements have been met. Pennsylvania received that certification on September 22, 2025.

In fact, Pennsylvania has built 54 EV charging stations using NEVI funds so far – more than double the number of any other state.

PennDOT’s community charging program supports both Level 2 and DC fast charging. Its published program minimum requirements include at least four ports per proposed station, at least 6 kW per port, two ADA-compliant parking spaces, and J1772 or CCS connectors on every port. Equipment must also meet Buy America requirements.

PennDOT lists 71 awards in this southeastern round as part of its roughly $100 million statewide community charging effort.

Applications for the western region close November 20. Central and eastern Pennsylvania applications close March 12, 2027.

thanks for posting. PA continues to lead the country in turning this program into actual chargers. The statewide coverage is night and day from just 2-3 years ago.

For the southeastern projects, PennDOT’s estimated schedule puts environmental reviews in November 2026 through January 2027, followed by agreement execution in January and February. Drivers will still have to wait for construction and commissioning before these awards become places to plug in.

#4674. Relaxed bear wins award for luxurious eating style—underneath an Alaskan waterfall

Published Nov 4, 2026 11:13 AM EST

Typically, when a bear catches a nutritious salmon, they don’t eat it under a rushing waterfall. But one unnamed black bear (Ursus americanus) eating at Anan Creek in Alaska’s Tongass National Forest decided to park underneath a waterfall and enjoy his fishy snack.

For this culinary innovation, the U.S. Forest Service team at Tongass National Forest has awarded the unnamed bear with the 2026 Shower Beer award.

“After watching this relaxed black bear gnawing on a salmon under rushing waters, we’re wondering if it might catch on—like the ursine equivalent of the shower beer,” the team writes. “The more you watch, the more sense it makes. No mess and no need to move to start fishing again. This bear may be on to something.”

The rangers at Tongass National Forest are currently awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory over the summer.

Tongass is the largest national forest in the United States, and covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the capital city of Juneau. The area includes Mendanhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), hiking trails, eagles soaring above, and plenty of bears. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears and eight brown bears (Ursus arctos). Like their beefy counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return annually each summer to eat salmon and teach their cubs how to fish and survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own habits and quirks.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted here, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their behavior.

#4673. Yangwang U9 Xtreme Breaks Its Own Top Speed Record With 312.7-MPH One-Way Run

It’s the first production vehicle to surpass 500 kilometers per hour.

China’s Yangwang U9 Xtreme hypercar already held the record for fastest production car, but it seems the company wasn’t satisfied with that. The U9 Xtreme just beat itself—and crossed the 500 kilometer-per-hour barrier doing it.

With German racing driver Marc Bessing behind the wheel (the same man who piloted the car for its previous records), the U9 Xtreme hit 503.2 km/h during a run in Abu Dhabi on November 1. That’s 312.7 miles per hour. Unlike the previous record of 496.2 km/h (308.3 mph) that was set at Germany’s Papenberg track, this time, Yangwang took its electric hypercar to a closed public road; about six miles of Sheikh Khalifa Bin Zayed International Road was closed for the record run.

“Unlike a dedicated test track, a public road presents a different set of challenges, making precision, stability and confidence in the vehicle more important than ever,” Besseng said. “Breaking a world record once is extraordinary but doing it again in such a different environment is truly special.”

The road itself required sweeping prior to each run, and Yangwang spent two days running on the road before setting the record on the final pass. The company says it inspected every meter of the path for potential debris, even picking up rogue wire particles that could’ve been deposited from the cleaning brushes sweeping up.

Both the FIA and Guinness World Records have recognized the record as the highest speed achieved by a production car in a single-direction run. Updates to the car are credited for breaking the 500 km/h barrier versus last year’s 496.2 km/h run: Yangwang says it adjusted the angle of the rear wing to increase rear downforce, tweaked the suspension software to increase rebound damping “in response to subtle undulations in parts of the road,” and, changed tire pressure to increase high-speed stability.

In case you were wondering, the U9 Xtreme is fitted with four electric motors producing more than 2958 horsepower. It uses a 1200-volt battery pack, which is an upgrade over the regular U9’s 800-volt pack. As for the tire, Yangwang says it uses a specially designed tire from Giti Tire. Yangwang itself is a subsidiary of BYD, China’s largest automaker.

The next closest car to the U9 Xtreme is the Bugatti Chiron Super Sport that hit 304.8 mph back in 2019. In other words, Yangwang didn’t need to set this latest record to take back the crown. It simply ran the car for the love of the game, and of course to break that 500 km/h barrier.

The video is a fascinating watch, as Bessing spends plenty of time warming the tires and brakes before going for the run. He keeps it at about half or a little over half throttle until he gets past 380 km/h. From there on out, it’s full throttle as the car flies up to 480 km/h and creeps the rest of the way up to—and beyond—500 km/h.

#4672. Losing Weight in Your 50s May Protect Your Heart Health Later in Life

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Losing weight in your 50s, even a modest amount, may help protect your heart health later in life, according to new research.Adults who lost weight in their early 50s saw their blood pressure, “good” cholesterol and inflammation change at about the same rate as adults who stayed at a healthy weight, according to a study from researchers at University College London and the University of Glasgow.Adults who gained weight in their early 50s saw those same measures worsen faster by their early 60s, the researchers reported. The authors posted the study on a research-sharing website on September 4. Other scientists have not yet peer-reviewed the work.

Charis Bridger-Staatz, PhD, a senior research fellow at UCL, led the study. She told Healthline the main takeaway for adults over 50 was that “it’s not too late to try and do things that are going to improve your health.”Nearly half of U.S. adults ages 40 to 59 had obesity from 2021 to 2023, the highest rate of any adult age group, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Among all U.S. adults, around 31.7% were overweight, according to the CDC.

The findings can apply to Americans because British and U.S. adults share similar weight patterns, said Solveig Cunningham, PhD, a professor of global health at Emory University’s Rollins School of Public Health. Cunningham, who was not involved in the research, told Healthline that Americans tend to gain weight across adulthood.

“By the time you get into your 50s, close to the majority of Americans already have obesity. Many others have overweight,” she said.The World Health Organization (WHO) calls obesity a chronic disease. Healthcare professionals diagnose overweight and obesity using a person’s weight and height, or body mass index (BMI).

Bridger-Staatz said the team set out to learn who lost weight and kept it off before GLP-1 weight loss medications became available, and whether that weight loss improved health over time.

She said researchers had long assumed that “once people had become overweight or developed obesity, people didn’t really lose weight and certainly not sustained it.”The team also asked, she said, “can we try and say something positive about health that isn’t just this kind of like doom and gloom?”The researchers used the British 1958 National Child Development Study, which has followed about 17,500 people born during one week in 1958. Of those, 6,309 took part in a health check in their early 60s, according to the report.The team compared each person’s highest weight between ages 23 and 42 with their weight between ages 50 and 55. Researchers sorted people by whether they gained or lost more than 5% of their body weight and kept the change. For a 200-pound person, 5% equals 10 pounds.To track heart health, the team compared blood tests and blood pressure readings at ages 44 and 62 with those of people who maintained a healthy weight.“We know everyone’s heart health is kind of going to get a little bit worse over that time because you are aging and that’s expected,” Bridger-Staatz said. The question, she said, was, “Does it slow the rate at which people’s heart health is getting worse?”

Weight loss slowed the decline in heart health for people who were overweight and for people with obesity, according to the report.People who were overweight and lost weight had the strongest positive results. By age 62, their body fat-to-lean tissue ratio matched that of the healthy-weight group. The authors wrote that differences in body fat may partly explain why weight changes affected heart health.People with obesity who lost weight had less body fat at 62 than people in the other obesity groups, according to the report.Sudhakara Chennareddy, MD, prevention cardiologist in the Center for Cardiovascular Prevention, Metabolism and Lipids at Georgia Heart Institute, told Healthline those results are what he’d expect. He was not involved in the research.“Even losing 5% has beneficial effects on the cardiovascular side effects,” he said. Long-term blood sugar was the exception. For people with obesity who lost weight, it rose more than in the healthy-weight group, though the authors reported that the result was not statistically significant.

A 2025 study of more than 15,000 U.S. adults, published in Endocrinology, Diabetes & Metabolism, found that adults who had previously had obesity tended to have higher blood sugar than those who had never had it, even after their BMI dropped.

“It’s not the patient’s fault… We need to treat this one like any other chronic disease, like we treat hypertension or we treat diabetes,” Chennareddy said.Compared with the healthy-weight group, people who gained weight in their early 50s had faster increases in blood pressure, blood fats, and inflammation, and declines in “good” cholesterol. Obesity is a chronic metabolic disease that leads to inflammation in the body, which can raise the risk of heart attack and stroke and worsen cholesterol levels, Chennareddy said. “The more weight they gain, they develop prediabetes and diabetes and fatty liver disease as well,” he said.These changes were largest for people who developed obesity or already had obesity and gained more weight, the researchers reported. This group also saw faster increases in long-term blood sugar levels.About 37% of participants gained more than 5% of their body weight in their early 50s. Only about 6% lost weight and kept it off, according to the study.“To me, that’s sort of the stronger message,” Cunningham said of the findings. Her advice for adults in their 50s is to avoid gaining weight.

People with obesity who lost and then gained the weight back saw faster drops in “good” cholesterol and faster rises in inflammation and long-term blood sugar.

By age 62, they weighed slightly less, on average, than people whose obesity remained steady, according to the report’s data. They also carried more body fat and had more inflammation.Weight cycling can do more harm than steady weight, Chennareddy said. He gave the example of someone who gains 20 pounds, loses 30 and then gains 20 again. “That is even more detrimental,” he said.When people lose weight, the body slows its resting metabolism, he said. When the weight comes back, “most of the weight they gain is fat, not muscle,” he said. Even someone who loses and regains 5% to 7% of their body weight may end up with slightly less muscle and more fat, he said.Some research has shown that weight fluctuation is associated with a higher risk of high blood pressure and cardiovascular disease-related death.

The study’s weight changes took place between about 2008 and 2013, according to the study’s timeline.

Wegovy, a GLP-1 medication for weight management, launched in the United Kingdom in September 2023, according to the UK Department of Health and Social Care.Cunningham said the weight-cycling findings raised questions for people who take GLP-1 medications. She said drugmakers’ own data show that “once you get off of those, your weight is going to go right back to where it was before, possibly even worse.”That could create the same up-and-down pattern, Cunningham said. She added that researchers don’t yet know “what happens in the really long term” for people who take these medications.

The study showed links between weight changes and heart health and cannot prove that weight changes caused the results, according to the authors. They wrote that the small number of people who lost weight made those results less precise.Bridger-Staatz also said the team did not look at why or how people lost weight.

Cunningham said adults lose muscle and bone mass with age, and that the loss is especially pronounced for women in their 50s and older. “Maintaining muscles and maintaining bones is so, so important,” she said.Staying active helps people keep muscle, even without weight loss, Cunningham said. “Even a little bit of activity…just keep moving,” she said.GLP-1 medications work best as part of a “comprehensive plan,” Chennareddy said. With his patients, he said he recommends continuous improvement rather than setting a goal to lose a specific amount of weight within a set period.Patients who treat weight loss as “a gradual process” do better long term, he said.“The most important thing is not to do fad diets,” Chennareddy said.For people losing weight, Chennareddy recommended:

Anyone considering changes to their weight can talk with a healthcare professional about their weight history and goals.

#4671. BYD’s flagship luxury EV with 1,000+ km of range hits 4,000 sales in just 19 days

BYD wasted no time, with sales of its new flagship electric sedan reaching 4,000 in just 19 days since its launch.

With a record of more than 300,000 electric vehicles sold last month, BYD sold more EVs than the US did in the entire third quarter, combined.

A big part of the higher demand is thanks to BYD’s latest breakthrough technology, including its second-generation Blade Batteries and Flash Charging technology.

BYD began equipping vehicles with the new battery and charging tech in March, and over the past six months it has posted higher year-over-year sales growth. Through October, BYD sold 1,953,700 vehicles, up 6% compared to the same period in 2025.

On October 13, BYD launched the Great Han, or “Da Han” in China, the first fully electric D-segment flagship sedan in its Dynasty lineup.

Just 19 days after its launch, BYD said Great Han EV sales reached 4,000 units. At that rate, sales could reach 10,000 or more in its first full month.

With “class-beating high value,” BYD said, “it has firmly established itself in the mid-to-high-end sedan segment above 250,000 yuan,” which is about $37,500.

The Great Han is available in three variants, priced from 235,900 yuan, or about $35,000. Buyers can choose from single- or dual-motor powertrains. The standard rear-wheel-drive (RWD) Premium trim offers up to 1,008 km (626 miles) of CLTC range, while the all-wheel-drive (AWD) Flagship variant offers up to 880 km (546 miles).

All models use a 102.326 kWh BYD Blade 2.0 battery pack. The RWD models have a single 370 kW (496 hp) motor, while the AWD variant adds a 200 kW (268 hp) front motor for a combined 570 kW (764 hp).

Like most of its new vehicles, the Great Han has a roof-mounted LiDAR and BYD’s God’s Eye B, a more advanced version of its intelligent driving system.

The ADAS system offers safety and convenience features, including Navigate on Autopilot on highways and in cities, plus remote autonomous parking.

All variants also include premium features, such as BYD’s DiSus-A dual-chamber air suspension system, rear-wheel steering, and zero-gravity front seats.

Measuring 5,256 mm in length, 1,999 mm in width, and 1,510 mm in height, with a 3,130 mm wheelbase, the Great Han is slightly bigger than the Tesla Model S and Lucid Air. It’s closer in size to the long-wheelbase Mercedes-Benz S-Class.

Thanks to BYD’s second-gen Blade Batteries and Flash Charging technology, the vehicle’s battery can charge from 10% to 70% in just 5 minutes. A full recharge (10% to 97%) takes just 9 minutes.

The Great Han joins the Great Tang SUV as the flagship sedan under BYD’s Dynasty lineup. BYD announced that Great Tang sales reached 14,000 units in October, marking four months of sales above 10,000.

#4670. Man builds robotic cat feeder that senses when dish is empty

Published Nov 4, 2026 12:00 PM EST

Pet owners can pick from any number of automatic cat feeders at this point, and even shell out hundreds of dollars for a particularly fancy kit. But at the end of the day, most of them are simply a scooper that dumps out premeasured amounts of feline food based on an internal timer.

Jason Winfield, a New Zealand-based YouTuber and frequent traveler, wanted a slightly more advanced option: a robotic cat feeder that distributes a predetermined amount of food for his two pals, and also senses when the dish is actually empty.

“I tried a few of those automatic feeders off-the-shelf, and look, they’re fine. They do the job. Sort of,” Winfield explains in his recent video. “But here’s what bothered me: How do I know my cat actually ate?”

Winfield’s invention is designed to avoid overfeeding or accidentally building a mountain of kibble. The device runs on a Raspberry Pi Pico with Wi-Fi capabilities, and includes a tiny LCD screen and a buzzer to alert when food has been delivered. An onboard real-time clock (RTC) module keeps time even without direct power, which allows for a timed feeding window for daily rations.

Winfield also attached a 3D-printed cat head toggle to cycle through settings on the feeder’s screen. DIY projects like this are bound to run into errors, so Winfield also encoded a failsafe that turns off the feed dispenser if the dish has remained full for a specific length of time.There’s even an ultrasonic sensor to detect the presence of a cat, so the feeder doesn’t inadvertently drop kibble on their head.

The end result is an efficient, reliable automatic feeder that keeps Winfield’s cats happy. Winfield himself is even confident that his cats will never go hungry while he’s traveling.

#4669. What does a blue Texas sweep mean for Elon Musk, Tesla & SpaceX?

After a historic election defeat in one of the most expensive elections in US election history, the state of Texas has turned blue. Along with this come potential implications for Elon Musk and his companies.

The US midterm election was yesterday, and ended up in a stunning result, with Democrats taking control of both houses of Congress by wide margins, and flipping seats that had been considered safe around the nation.

Perhaps most notably, many of these seats were in Texas – a republican stronghold which saw a clean sweep, with the Democrats winning every statewide contest. Republicans maintained some state legislative power and won the State Senate, but as of this writing Democrats are currently ahead in the count for the State House.

The highest profile contest was for Texas Senate, where James Talarico won by a 55-43 margin. This race set the record for the most expensive Senate race in the nation’s history, with over half a billion dollars spent on this one seat alone.

About half of the total money spent on the race came courtesy of republican PACs, a method by which companies and the ultra-wealthy can launder money into bribes to buy elections. And most of the PAC money in the race came from one man, Elon Musk, who spent $212 million to support the enormously unpopular and scandal-ridden outgoing Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton

That’s nearly half of the $474 million dollars that Musk put into this election cycle, suggesting that he saw this race of particular importance. And yet, his candidate lost miserably.

But the rout did not stop with Paxton. Paxton’s old job as AG is now going to be filled by Democrat Nathan Johnson. And Greg Abbott, the outgoing Governor, was defeated by Gina Hinojosa. Even the less high-profile races for court seats were swept by Democrats – three seats on the 15th Court of Appeals and four seats on the Texas Supreme Court.

And those results, even beyond the big-spending Senate race, could all matter quite a lot to Elon Musk.

In 2021, Musk announced that Tesla would move its headquarters to Texas, after Musk got in a spat with California government because he didn’t want to follow COVID restrictions for worker safety.

But the move wasn’t only about COVID restrictions – it was also about Musk’s vision of having more control over the business environment. And, by making allies with Ken Paxton and Greg Abbott, he has had quite a bit of control in Texas.

The two have rolled out the red carpet for Musk, giving him carte blanche in his adopted state.

Autonomous vehicle regulations have been changed, allowing driverless Robotaxis to operate where other states with more advanced regulations and transparency requirements would not. And many other laws benefitting Tesla and SpaceX have been passed. Paxton even sued Sam Altman, Musk’s chief AI rival, just weeks ago.

Perhaps more notably for Musk personally, Texas has promised to allow Musk to get away with more financial shenanigans than states with more established business regulations might.

With Tesla both headquartered and incorporated in Texas, it can now use special “business courts” instituted by Abbott at Musk’s own urging. If cases from these courts are appealed, they go to the 15th Court of Appeals, a court created by Abbott and filled with 3 hand-picked judges, intended to reduce the chance that a Democratic district court (say, one in Austin, whereTesla is headquartered) gets final say on any issue.

But, the 15th Court of Appeals just had elections last night – and its three seats were flipped to Democratic control.

The 15th Court of Appeals also, just last week, stopped an inquiry into thousands of pages of emails between Abbott and Musk. The emails had been released, but are heavily redacted, with Abbott referring to the redacted portions as having “intimate” information in them.

And who made that request for inquiry into the emails? Gina Hinojosa, a name you might recognize, as she is the next Governor of Texas, as of last night.

As of yet, those emails have not all been released, so we don’t actually know exactly how much influence Musk was able to exercise over the state’s outgoing Governor. But given the changes we know about, the money Musk spent in Texas, and the thousands of pages of emails that have been redacted, it seems likely that there is something more to be found in them.

So what does this all mean for Tesla, our main area of coverage here at Electrek?

On a Texas state level, probably not all that much. There’s no reason that Democrats in the state would interfere with Tesla’s production of electric vehicles – in fact, they’d probably encourage it more than republicans do. Talarico has stated that he supports Tesla – it is a large employer in the state, after all.

And certainly, the national wins by Democrats could be a boon for EVs, and for climate action, given how hostile republicans have been to them (and Musk has been the single largest supporter of that hostility towards EVs, which has cost Tesla billions).

The same likely goes for SpaceX – perhaps a blue Texas will be more restrictive of the company’s improper usage of protected habitats, or building of data centers, or whatever the hell is going on on twitter. But the core businesses of space launches and Starlink don’t seem likely to go anywhere.

For Elon Musk, though, things could be different. Given his “intimate” relationship with Abbott, the extreme amounts of money he spent on Paxton, and the highly personal nature of his truly ridiculous attacks against Talarico, it seems unlikely that he will have a similar level of allyship with Texas government actors as he did in prior years. Talarico’s main anti-corruption message was seemingly aimed straight at Musk’s attempts to buy elections, after all.

And given his high levels of spending on a party that is outright hostile electric vehicles, it seems clear that his personal fortunes are far more important to him than the well-being of his companies.

as a texan, I had zero faith that talrico would win, especially with the amount of money musk dumped in the race at the last minute. I’m so heartened to see that money cannot buy everything and that we, as a country, are finally pushing back against the trump/musk insanity. maybe we can start upholding the constitution and ensuring the law applies to all citizens regardless of wealth.

This is all important to note, because Musk has been working towards a scheme to merge SpaceX and Tesla, a deal which would likely be a detriment to both companies and all of their shareholders. Musk wants the deal so he can exercise more control over, and extract more personal wealth from, the combined entity.

But that scheme could rely on a favorable legal environment in Texas courts, an environment that just got less favorable.

And, given Musk’s penchant for childish lashings-out anytime he deems people insufficiently obsequious to his imagined greatness, could we see another situation where Musk encounters the tiniest amount of pushback from state government and then picks up his toys and leaves, as he already did in both California and Delaware? Time will have to tell. Keep your popcorn buckets primed and ready.

#4668. EcoFlow’s new DELTA Gen4 portable power stations keep a reserve of extra power for emergencies

Published Nov 4, 2026 1:24 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›

If you’ve ever driven with white knuckles to a gas station while your car’s range read “0 miles,” you’ll appreciate a new feature on this portable power station. EcoFlow is building a similar cushion into its new DELTA Gen4 portable power stations. A feature called Emergency Power Mode holds back a small reserve for charging phones after the screen hits 0 percent.

Two models are on sale today through EcoFlow’s website: the DELTA 3000 Gen4 at an early-bird $1,299 and the DELTA 3800 Gen4 at $1,699, against list prices of $1,699 and $2,199. Both put out 3,600 watts in chassis EcoFlow says are smaller and lighter than its DELTA 3 Ultra models, which include the DELTA 3 Ultra Plus we tried last year. They arrive a month after EcoFlow’s TITAN home batteries targeted whole-home backup.

A power station spends some charge just keeping its inverter awake. EcoFlow rates both DELTA Gen4 models at 14 watts with the AC outlets switched on and nothing plugged in, and 3 watts in standby. At 14 watts, a full day of idling uses 336 watt-hours, about 11 percent of the DELTA 3000 Gen4’s 3,072Wh battery.

The 3-watt standby number is what lets EcoFlow claim a fully charged DELTA 3800 Gen4 can sit for about 52 days before it drains, which matters for one parked in a closet waiting for an outage. EcoFlow pairs the lower overhead with a mode called Fridge Runtime Boost and rates the DELTA 3000 Gen4 for up to 58 hours of refrigerator runtime. The DELTA 3800 Gen4 gets more than 70 hours.

Those fridge numbers come from EcoFlow’s own tests with an empty 654-liter Samsung refrigerator, and the company notes that food load, room temperature, and door openings all change the result. The mode also supports one compressor-based appliance, such as a fridge or freezer, at a time, and EcoFlow says not to run other AC loads alongside it. We haven’t tested either DELTA Gen4 model yet, so these performance figures are EcoFlow’s. Emergency Power Mode covers what’s left after the battery runs down. You turn it on from the unit or the EcoFlow app, and EcoFlow says the reserve can give an iPhone 17 nearly a full extra charge.

Both DELTA Gen4 models share a 16.8 x 11.4-inch footprint, and both are rated for 3,600 watts continuous and 7,200 watts of surge from their 120V outlets. That’s enough to run a 1,500-watt space heater and a refrigerator at the same time with room to spare. EcoFlow’s original DELTA Pro weighed about 99 pounds to hit the same 3,600-watt rating.

The DELTA 3800 Gen4 fits 691 extra watt-hours and about 10 more pounds into the same footprint, for 3,763Wh at 67.5 pounds. EcoFlow says that’s roughly 33 pounds lighter than the DELTA Pro, and it holds slightly more energy. The DELTA 3000 Gen4 holds 3,072Wh at 57.3 pounds, and EcoFlow puts it at about 20 percent lighter than the DELTA 3 Ultra, with the same capacity.

The bigger model also has more ways to grow. The DELTA 3800 Gen4 takes up to 2,000 watts of solar across two inputs and has an expansion port for up to two extra batteries, including the DELTA Pro 3 Smart Extra Battery, for about 12kWh total. The DELTA 3000 Gen4 has one 1,000-watt solar input, and its spec sheet lists no battery port.

EcoFlow says the DELTA 3000 Gen4 refills from a wall outlet in under two hours and the DELTA 3800 Gen4 in under 2.5 hours. The 3kWh, 3,600-watt class is crowded, with Anker’s SOLIX F3000 and Jackery’s Explorer 3000 v2 at the same capacity and output. Our guide to the best portable power stations covers the field.

The DELTA 3000 Gen4 and DELTA 3800 Gen4 are listed for preorder. As of November 4, EcoFlow shows the DELTA 3800 Gen4 shipping in late November and the DELTA 3000 Gen4 in early December.

EcoFlow’s early-bird pricing runs through December 7. That puts the DELTA 3800 Gen4 at $1,699, 23 percent off its $2,199 list, and the DELTA 3000 Gen4 at $1,299, which is $400 below its $1,699 list.

For a house that needs a fridge, a router, and a few lamps through a weekend outage, this is the DELTA to look at first. It has the same 3,600-watt output as its bigger sibling and weighs about 10 pounds less. The savings come out of expandability, since it gets one 1,000-watt solar input, four charging methods, and no listed battery expansion.

At early-bird prices, $400 more buys 691 extra watt-hours, a second 1,000-watt solar input, and an expansion port that takes the system to about 12kWh with add-on batteries. That port is the reason to step up if you plan to expand a home-backup system later. EcoFlow rates it for more than 70 hours on a refrigerator and lists six ways to charge it.

#4667. Why Cancer Biomarker Testing Is Personal for Mark-Paul Gosselaar

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Known for his iconic roles on “Saved by the Bell,” “NYPD Blue,” “Franklin & Bash,” and “Found,” Mark-Paul Gosselaar knows how to grab an audience.

Now, he’s using that star power to raise awareness about cancer biomarker testing while sharing how he prioritizes his own health and well-being.

“Health is a huge thing for my wife and I, and our family,” Gosselaar told Healthline. “We are constantly aware of new technologies.”

Having seen people in his life navigate cancer diagnoses, Gosselaar is now raising awareness about the role of biomarker testing in cancer treatment through his partnership with AstraZeneca and its Meet Your Mark campaign.

The campaign aims to educate people facing cancer diagnoses and their loved ones about how biomarker testing may help doctors make more informed, personalized treatment decisions. It also encourages patients to discuss testing with their healthcare teams.

“Biomarkers may tell doctors the specific type of cancer present and if targeted therapies or immunotherapy might help,” Mark Socinski, MD, oncologist and Executive Medical Director of the AdventHealth Cancer Institute, told Healthline.

He explained that biomarkers are typically genes or proteins that doctors measure through blood or tissue tests. They are used to help guide treatment in numerous diseases but are especially powerful tools in many types of cancer.

“They help decode why cancers behave differently, even when two people have the same cancer type,” said Socinski. “However, while biomarker testing provides useful information, it does not guarantee a specific outcome.”

Despite those limitations, Socinski sees promise in the shift from one-size-fits-all cancer treatment to care tailored to each patient’s specific cancer characteristics.

“Biomarker testing does play a critical role here, and it is important for people to be aware of the potential benefits,” Socinski said. “It may help change the course of a person’s treatment journey.”

Gosselaar hopes that greater awareness of biomarker testing can help people facing a cancer diagnosis feel more informed about their treatment options.

“A lot of the time, when a loved one or someone who has been diagnosed with cancer [it can] feel like your world is in a tailspin,” he said. “I wanted to get the word out for anyone who’s going through a cancer diagnosis, or a caretaker, to know that biomarker testing is an option, because even though two cancers are similar, their tumors can act very differently and biomarker testing may help the medical expert with more personalized treatment.”

As part of the campaign, Gosselaar took part in a commercial, something he hadn’t done since before his days on “Saved by the Bell.”

“This was the first time that I actually had to be on set and not be a character; I had to be me talking about this very serious issue,” he said.

While it was a challenging experience, he said it was also fulfilling.

“I enjoyed the process, and to be able to use my platform to be able to spread the word; it means a lot to me,” he said. “I’m very selective of the things that I want to attach myself to, and this seemed like the right fit.”

He particularly enjoyed recreating Zack Morris’s signature “timeout” gesture from “Saved by the Bell,” which allowed his character to freeze time and speak directly to the camera.

“Using something from the past that was such a symbolic gesture to so many people of my generation that are now my age and possibly going through [cancer] or knowing someone who’s going through [cancer to] direct them to [this campaign], means a lot,” he said.

Beyond his efforts to raise awareness about cancer biomarker testing, Gosselaar is equally focused on taking care of his own health.

Getting quality sleep is one of his top priorities. He sleeps on a high-tech mattress that monitors sleep stages, heart rate, heart rate variability, and respiratory rate. He also uses a biometric health and fitness tracker, prioritizes healthy eating, and uses saunas and red light therapy.

“We do everything that we possibly can, but I’m less about longevity and more about just living a healthy lifestyle,” Gosselaar said. “I want to continue doing the things that I’ve done since I was a child…without feeling held back by my health.”

As he embraces his 50s, he said he’d like to live a long life for his children and future grandchildren. He started taking his health seriously in his 40s after undergoing shoulder surgery.

“[It] really made me realize [that] all the damage I had done in my 20s and 30s sort of adds up later in life, and that’s probably something that I would tell the younger me… to preserve a little bit more and take [an] approach that recovery is just as important as the workout because I did not use my recovery very well; it was not a priority for me,” said Gosselaar.

He also makes time for himself every day. He said doing so makes him a better person and more able to care for his wife and four children.

“[It’s] something that I believe in; that I need to do something for myself before I can do something for someone else. Or if I do something for someone else, then I have to equalize that by doing something for me,” he said.

Daily physical activity also helps support his mental well-being.

“I need to do something where I challenge myself, and it could be as simple as a walk. It could be as simple as just getting outside and lifting something heavy [or] taking bags of groceries and taking the long way into your house,” Gosselaar said.

“Like challenging yourself with picking up things, you know, taking backpacks from the car from your kids and seeing if you can carry three in one hand…or going into the gym and spending an hour in the gym, or 30 minutes, or just moving.”

When he’s in the sauna, he works on breathing and clearing his thoughts.

“Some people need to meditate, some people need to talk to somebody. I encourage all of that because I think all of that helps,” he said.

“I’ve done them all. I’ve done the cold plunging, I’ve done all that stuff…some of it works, and some of it doesn’t; it’s whatever you believe in. So I just encourage people to stay healthy and move, get outside, and help other people.”

#4666. Audi May Invest an Additional $3 Billion in Georgia Factory: Report

The German automaker just announced its $4 billion plans for its first U.S. plant, but it may already be considering a second phase of construction.

Audi hasn’t even broken ground on its newly announced $4 billion plans for a 1500-acre factory in Macon, Georgia, but the German automaker is already hinted at an additional $3 billion investment in the facility.

A new report from Reuters claims that Audi is already considering a second phase of construction at the Georgia plant. After pledging to invest an initial $4 billion, documents released by the Mid-Georgia Gateway Development Authority reportedly state that Audi will invest $3 billion more by 2033. Audi supposedly aims to employ an additional 3000 workers as part of the expansion plan.

The Trump Administration allegedly promised Audi some degree of tariff relief as part of the decision to build its first U.S. production facility; Reuters reported that Audi pushed for the European Union import duty to be lowered to 7.5 percent, but that the U.S. Commerce Department was expected to agree to around 10 percent. Currently, Audi imports all of its models to the U.S. from Europe and Mexico, and models from the EU are subject to a 15 percent tariff. Audi paid $1.4 billion in duties to the U.S. government last year.

Georgia is heavily incentivizing Audi’s decision to build in the Peach State: it is giving Audi the land, as well as providing $458 million in tax incentives and offering $120 million in grants. These grants will focus on infrastructure, rail improvements, environmental site remediation, and construction, according to Automotive News. The company will also be provided an additional $430 million in subsidies for water, road improvements, utility issues, workforce training, and recruitment.

Audi plans to produce its Q7, Q8, and Q9 SUVs at its future U.S. facilities. The German automaker isn’t limiting its U.S. production plans to Georgia, either: an additional 25,000 Audi units will reportedly be produced at an incoming Scout Motors factory in South Carolina. Audi pledged to build 200,000 vehicles annually at the Georgia plant by the early 2030s.

#4665. Tesla accused of selling FSD to Korean owners who can’t legally use it

A South Korean consumer group is asking regulators to stop Tesla from marketing “Full Self-Driving” to customers whose cars can’t legally run it. By Tesla’s own numbers, that covers 99% of the Teslas it sold in Korea last year.

Citizens United for Consumer Sovereignty plans to file the complaint with the Korea Fair Trade Commission (KFTC) on Thursday, according to Reuters, which reviewed it. It comes just a week after a Seoul court threw out a refund lawsuit from Korean owners who paid for FSD.

It all comes down to where the car was built. The Model S, Model X, and Cybertruck come from US factories and enter Korea under the KORUS free trade agreement, which recognizes US safety standards. Those are the only Teslas that got “FSD (Supervised)” when Tesla switched it on in Korea late last year.

The problem is that those don’t represent the vast majority of Tesla vehicles sold in Korea.

The Model 3 and Model Y sold in Korea come from Giga Shanghai. There’s no equivalent deal with China, so those cars need Korean approval that FSD doesn’t have.

And that’s most of the fleet. Tesla Korea country manager Seo Young-deuk told lawmakers last month that FSD works on about 20% of Teslas registered in the country. Tesla has sold more than 170,000 Shanghai-built vehicles in Korea since 2023, per data it handed to the National Assembly, and sales of those China-made cars grew more than fivefold between 2023 and 2025.

Seo’s figure also clears up the conflicting eligibility numbers we flagged when Korean police booked 80 Tesla drivers for using illegal FSD unlock devices last month. A lawmaker’s data from May put it at 2.4%, while a data firm counted 20.7% in August. Tesla’s own testimony matches the higher one.

For years, Tesla charged Korean buyers a one-time 9.043 million won (about $6,726) for FSD. It moved to a 150,000 won ($112) monthly subscription in August.

The complaint points to Tesla’s “coming soon” promotion last year and a demo video shot on Korean roads. Neither made it clear that FSD would only work on a small slice of the cars Tesla was selling. The group says Tesla knew that and kept pitching the package to every buyer anyway.

“Tesla generated substantial revenue by selling an expensive driver-assistance system to mass-market buyers who cannot use it for even a single day,” said Choi Young-suk, who heads automotive issues at the group.

It wants the KFTC to temporarily order Tesla to stop marketing FSD for ineligible cars. It’s also asking for fines and for the case to be sent to state investigators.

The KFTC is already looking at this. An official told Reuters the agency opened a probe into Tesla’s FSD advertising earlier this year and has received written responses from the company. Tesla didn’t respond to Reuters’ requests for comment.

Tesla has collected FSD money from buyers of China-made cars in Korea for more than three years. But at an October 8 parliamentary hearing, Seo testified that Tesla had never formally asked the transport ministry to test FSD. Tesla filed for certification about two weeks later.

Approval won’t be a rubber stamp either. The ministry told a lawmaker that FSD doesn’t comply with local safety rules, including the requirement that drivers keep their hands on the wheel. Current FSD versions let drivers go hands-free as long as the cabin camera sees them watching the road.

None of this slowed sales. Tesla passed BMW this year to become Korea’s top imported car brand.

So far, owners haven’t had much luck in court. Last month, a Seoul court dismissed a lawsuit from Tesla owners seeking FSD refunds, with the judge pointing to Korean regulations, not Tesla, as the reason more features never launched.

#4664. California has way more bugs than we thought

Published Nov 4, 2026 2:00 PM EST

It’s true that there are more insects on Earth than any other animal. They make up roughly 80 percent of the planet’s animals and include about 900,000 known species. However, those jaw-dropping numbers can make it easy to undercount our six-legged friends. Take the state of California. Over 60,000 different species of insects reside in the Golden State, and scientists have only described about two-thirds of them. A study published today in the journal Ecography details the findings, which represents a huge bump in the estimated number of insects in California.

The study is part of the California Insect Barcode Initiative (CIBI), a $6 million project to collect and identify every species of insect in the state. Multiple institutions including the California Department of Food and Agriculture, UC Berkeley, UC Riverside, San Diego Natural History Museum, the California Academy of Sciences in San Francisco, and Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County (NHM) worked together to DNA barcode over one million insect specimens.

To build the insect library, the team gathered tissue samples from museum collections and caught living insects in 72 ecoregions around the state. Ecoregions are places that have similar ecosystems as defined by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). They also undertook research expeditions to 454 additional locations across California, and used Malaise traps to gather the insects. Malaise traps passively capture bugs, but require a bit of work to maintain.

“This is an example of community science. Volunteers stepped forward to help with sampling by managing traps, which we would not have been able to do for continuous weekly sampling,” Giar-Ann Kung, a study co-author and NHM Entomology collections manager, said in a statement.

The study looked at Level 3 ecoregions, which include places like the Mojave Basin and Range, Southern California Mountains, and Sierra Nevada. They found that the Mojave Basin and Range have the highest insect species richness.

The team also compared parallel ecoregions and found that each one is home to its own unique mix of insect life, even if they have a similar climate and geography. While there are parallels between locations within the same ecoregion, the team found that the richness of life across California is more abundant and more delicate than previously thought. Researchers say that these results highlight the need for more aggressive conservation of California’s wild places to protect the insects living there.

#4663. Kia EV7 revealed as an upcoming midsize electric SUV

Kia is crushing it with a full lineup of electric vehicles ranging from entry-level SUVs to the three-row EV9 and PV5 van. A leaked document revealed that Kia plans to add the EV7, a new midsize electric SUV, to fill the gap between the EV6 and the three-row EV9.

With 291,219 vehicles sold last month, up 10.3% from October 2025, Kia posted its eighth consecutive month of year-over-year sales growth.

Kia said it plans to build on the momentum by focusing on electrified vehicles in key markets, including hybrids in the US and fully electric vehicles in Europe.

After launching the EV2 earlier this year, Kia now offers one of the most complete EV lineups, including the EV2, EV3, EV4, EV5, EV6, EV9, and PV5 van.

According to a recently leaked document, a new midsize electric SUV will join the lineup. KoreanCarBlog uncovered an internal document from Kia’s Employment Stability Committee that reveals the company’s upcoming production plans.

The report claims “production of mid-range electric SUV ‘EV7’ to proceed” at Kia’s Gwangju factory in South Korea.

Although no other details were revealed, the EV7 will be a midsize electric SUV, slotted between the EV6 and three-row EV9.

During its 2026 CEO Investor Day in April, Kia announced plans to expand its EV lineup to 14 models by 2030.

In Europe, Kia plans for EVs to account for 66% of sales by 2030, with a full lineup that includes the EV2, EV3, EV4, EV5, EV6, EV9, three PBVs, a new C-segment electric SUV, and its first “SDV B-segment hatchback.”

So what can we expect from the upcoming EV7? Kia said earlier this year that it’s developing a new EV platform “to significantly enhance both product performance and cost competitiveness.”

Although it didn’t offer specifics, Kia claimed the new EV platform delivers up to a 40% increase in battery capacity and a 9% improvement in motor output.

It will use Kia’s fifth-generation batteries, providing up to 15% higher energy density than its current tech.

Kia’s upcoming software-defined vehicles (SDVs) are expected to integrate Hyundai’s SDV architecture (CODA), Pleos Connect infotainment system, and Gleo AI, an in-vehicle Agenic AI.They will also have Level 2++ autonomous driving capabilities on highways.

The EV5, Kia’s current midsize electric SUV, is 4,615 mm long, 1,875 mm wide, and 1,675 mm tall, with a 2,750 mm wheelbase, which is about the size of the Sportage, so you can expect the EV7 to be slightly bigger. It will likely be closer in size to the Sorento.

Powered by an 81.4 kWh battery, the Kia’s current EV5 offers a WLTP range of up to 329 miles (530 km).

Not a full lineup, the EV van is still missing. Why offer so many different SUVs between Kia and Hyundai but no van/minivan?

However, unlike the EV6 and EV9, the EV5 uses a 400V electrical architecture rather than an 800V. As a result, charging the battery from 10% to 80% takes about 30 minutes, rather than 18 to 25 minutes. The upcoming EV7 will likely use the 800V system for faster charging.

The document also revealed Kia will begin production of “completely redesigned models” at its Gwangmyeong Factory, including the 2028 Carnival Hybrid and a hydrogen-powered Carnival by 2029.

At its Gyeonggi Hwaseong Factory, Kia will reportedly also produce redesigned models, including the Sorento Hybrid in 2028.

#4662. Why a pink potato-like robot is wheeling around Philadelphia

Published Nov 4, 2026 2:17 PM EST

It was a showdown worthy of a classic Western, except the things rolling down the street weren’t tumbleweeds. They were robots.

On one side of an Old City sidewalk in Philadelphia, an Uber Eats robot trundled along on its daily route. Suddenly, something blocked its path, and it was met face-to-interface with another, new robot. This new bot on the block was wildly different from its utilitarian, food-conveying counterpart: Not only did it have blond hair, blue eyes, and a perpetually lolling tongue, but it also had a name. Meet Orifice the Awebot.

Meg Saligman, founder of the Ministry of Awe, an immersive art installation located in a 19th-century Old City bank building, had raced ahead to intercept the bot so Orifice could meet it. According to The Philadelphia Inquirer, Orifice’s creator, Madison Polidoro, then joked that the two robots were “gonna fight!”

The Uber Eats robot chose a pacifist approach, steering around its would-be adversary without incident.

But Orifice wasn’t created to instigate a territorial dispute between robots. She was made to promote peace between robots and humans, which is no small feat in the City of Brotherly Love. Here, delivery bots aren’t brothers. They’re the “other,” even when they’re bringing you a cheesesteak with Whiz.

Since Uber Eats delivery bots made their Philadelphia debut in March, the city has not exactly rolled out the red carpet. Within weeks of the robots’ launch, Philadelphians displayed “the whole spectrum” of reactions, according to Dr. Philip Dames, an associate professor of mechanical engineering at Temple University in Philly.  Most people barely gave them a second glance, but on the extreme end, one robot was kicked over at around midnight, and one was sat on and graffitied with the words, “DESTROY ME PLZ.”

Orifice was designed to be a more warmhearted, interactive answer to the joyless functionality of delivery bots. But why are some people compelled to harass delivery bots in the first place? And can a pink potato with a tongue change that?

The Ministry commissioned Polidoro, a Philadelphia-area fine artist and fabricator known as 10 Ton Fetus for her surreal and psychological sculptures, to create a mobile sculpture.

After talking it over with her colleagues, she decided to build her own robot, Orifice, as a foil to the Uber Eats bots.

“Having run into them, and being horrified by it, I was excited at the prospect of making their archnemesis, a hero of sorts!” she says. “Something perfectly opposite of what they [delivery robots] are.”

Polidoro knew that to properly offset the slick, appliance-like look of the Uber Eats bots, she would need to give Orifice plenty of human flourishes.

“She had to be cute, friendly, and human,” Polidoro says. “I carefully considered approachability and anchoring points for human connection in her design.”

Orifice stands two feet tall and is shaped like a potato. She has pink, weatherproof rubber skin, and large blue eyes that blink regularly and can also be remotely operated. Her dangling tongue, tuft of Troll doll-esque blond hair, and pink ribbon juxtaposed with an occasional top hat give her a quirky, sometimes unsettling charm.

And yes, her name is literal: She has what Polidoro calls a “functional orifice” on her rear end, a common feature of the artist’s work.

For a city that has officially embraced the grotesque hockey mascot Gritty, which The Guardian has described as “an acid trip of a mascot,” Orifice almost seems like a love letter on wheels. And so far, the reaction to Orifice has been largely positive, Polidoro says.

“Most people smile, laugh and record her, asking questions and wanting to know more,” she says. “Occasionally, people are surprised or find her a bit unsettling. But even those people seem curious and lighthearted.”

Unlike the delivery bots, which Polidoro describes as “something from a science fiction novel,” Orifice seems to hit a sweet spot in terms of adorableness.

“She seems to tap into the psychology of cuteness, like a dog or a child, something understood to be precious and innocent,” she says. (Fortunately, Orifice seems to stop short of provoking “cute aggression,” the urge to squeeze something unbearably adorable.)

And there truly is a psychology of cuteness. Researchers have found that robots designed with the “baby schema” (big eyes, round faces, and other infant-like features) are perceived as cuter and more trustworthy. Research by Kate Darling, a robot ethicist who studied human/robot interaction at the MIT Media Lab for about 15 years, has also found that names and backstories make people hesitate to hurt robots, Dames notes. But a pretty face can only go so far.

“A face alone doesn’t protect a robot,” Dames says. “The Uber Eats rovers have blinking, winking eyes and still got hazed, and a face engineered to look friendly can read as manipulative.”

And that’s not the only way making a robot more “humanlike” can backfire, according to Dr. Donald Hantula, a professor of psychology and neuroscience at Temple University. He likens it to Star Wars’ beloved beep-bot R2-D2 versus the frequently beleaguered, all-too-humanoid C-3PO. The more a robot resembles us, he suggests, the more likely it is to face the bullying we usually reserve for one another.

“The problem is that the more human something becomes, the more we tend to treat it as human-like,” he says. “And we humans have a really terrible history of how we treat fellow members of our species.”

So, will Orifice manage to strike the perfect balance between human and machine, serving as an ambassador of goodwill between tech-weary humans and the machines rolling into their neighborhoods?

So, what is driving hostility toward robots on the street? Whatever it is, Philadelphia seems to have a lot of it. In 2015, hitchBOT, a robot built for a social experiment on the kindness of strangers, was found decapitated at the top of Old City’s Elfreth’s Alley. Named after local blacksmith and property owner Jeremiah Elfreth, the alley is considered one of the oldest continuously inhabited residential streets in the United States.

The alley’s museum has since hosted events about hitchBOT’s demise that are part commemoration, part celebration, with an annual festival possibly in the works.

But hostility toward robots is far from just a Philly thing, or even a delivery bot thing, Dames notes.

“I’d expect friction wherever robots enter public space without local say,” he told Popular Science.

That invasion of space without public buy-in can be especially challenging on crowded public sidewalks, which robots must share, as Dames puts it, “with kids, dogs, wheelchair users, and tourists, none of whom opted in.” On those packed sidewalks, the robots are, in Hantula’s words, “essentially beer coolers on wheels” and consistently “get in people’s way.”

What happens when driverless cars break the law?

Can apps really make you fluent in another language?

Do water picks really work? Dentists weigh in.

Beyond these logistical issues, Dames says, robots on the street are often among the only physical manifestations of the otherwise inaccessible corporate entities they represent.

“The robot is the only part of a company a person can physically reach,” he says. “You can’t confront a cloud algorithm or a board of directors, but you can confront the rover on your block.”

Facing down delivery bots is precisely what Dr. Carolyn Marvin, a retired University of Pennsylvania communications professor, has been doing. On Oct. 14, Marvin was arrested and cited for disorderly conduct after stationing herself in front of an Uber Eats robot near Reading Terminal Market. It wasn’t the first time she’d blocked the bots on her daily walks.

Marvin told KYW Newsradio that she’s protesting “the ruthless way that rich corporations are casting aside human workers.” She says she has no intention of stopping.

Confronting robots may also offer an outlet for modern anxieties about the rapid, seemingly ungovernable ascent of artificial intelligence, which some experts have warned could wipe out humanity within a decade. Some passersby have even been known to yell “clanker,” an insult popularized by Star Wars that has since become an anti-AI slur, at Uber Eats bots.

“The physical embodiment gives you a better target in a sense,” Hantula says. “It’s really hard to kick against AI, but it’s like, okay, I see that thing and I can.”

And some of it might be simply for show, Hantula notes.

“A lot of this I think is also driven by getting social media likes,” he says.

Yet some cultures do seem able to coexist peacefully with delivery bots and other robots. In Korea and Japan, for example, robots are viewed as reliable, time-saving helpers, not professional rivals or harbingers of doom.

Orifice probably won’t be able to single-handedly repair the troubled history of robot/human relations in America, but perhaps her presence will provide, as her name suggests, an opening.

“Sometimes it can be, and needs to be, as simple as a moment of raw discovery and joy, savoring the little things that make us human,” Polidoro says. “I’d like Orifice to bring a piece of that [joy and discovery] to everyone she encounters.”

#4661. The Iambic Model T Is the Luxury Sneaker Built for Life at the Racetrack

Our car experts choose every product we feature. We may earn money from the links on this page.

Italian leather, custom comfort, and auto-inspired design make these my favorite shoes for Formula 1 weekends.

There’s something fitting about the Model T sneaker becoming my favorite for race weekends. Much like the cars we obsess over, the Iambic Model T takes an engineering-first approach to comfort, combining modern technology, thoughtful construction, and premium materials.

Think of it like commissioning a luxury grand tourer. A Ferrari isn’t simply about horsepower; it’s about the materials, the craftsmanship, and attention to the person behind the wheel. Iambic applies the same philosophy, from its Italian leather to its personalized fit.

After wearing mine throughout the year, across Europe and the U.S., I'm convinced the approach works.

Rather than relying on conventional shoe sizing, Iambic uses AI-assisted technology to create a personalized fit. The process begins with a smartphone app that captures images of your feet and collects information about your comfort preferences. It may seem unusual, but I promise it makes sense. Through the app, you will send pictures of each foot from different angles to capture the full scope and how you stand. That data helps determine how your shoes are made. These foot scans showed me that I wear slightly more on my right side because of an old skating injury, something I never knew.

The Model T is handcrafted in Portugal using Italian full-grain leather, with a triple-layer rubber sole, adjustable foam insoles, and a padded heel collar. It’s an impressive combination.

For someone accustomed to appreciating the details inside a well-appointed Italian automobile, that approach feels familiar. The materials matter, but so does how everything works together.

I’ve worn my white Model Ts all over Modena’s cobblestone streets with my family, through multiple days at racetracks, and across America on my 36-hour Route 66 road trip. They’ve become my favorite driving and racing shoes, and that says a lot.

Anyone who’s attended a race knows how much walking it involves. Between navigating sprawling circuits, standing for hours, and sometimes carrying equipment or bags, your footwear gets a serious workout.

Silverstone was the ultimate test. Four consecutive days of traversing the circuit left my sneakers considerably dirty, but my feet stayed unswollen and blister-free. I didn’t even wear socks with them the last day (so they wouldn’t clash with my Fernando outfit). They were so comfortable that I rarely thought about my feet, even when walking across the hilly, uneven grounds and up and down the grandstand.

They also became my preferred driving shoes for long-haul trips with my cousin. Their fit and manageable sole made hours and hours in the driver’s seat enjoyable, without the bulk of traditional athletic sneakers. And despite the punishment they underwent, a basic leather-cleaning kit brought the white back to life.

At $600, the Model T belongs in the same conversation as other premium footwear, but the appeal goes beyond appearance. You’re investing in personalized construction, a sneaker designed for serious use and only for you. After a full season of travel, mine have more than justified their price.

With Austin, Texas, behind us and Las Vegas approaching, remember that a Grand Prix involves considerably more walking than most first-time attendees anticipate. Every year, social media fills with photos of blistered feet from fans who chose fashionable boots or sleek loafers over comfort. My advice? Save the fancy boots and dress shoes for dinner.

If you’re already investing in the experience of attending a Formula 1 race, or any race, the right footwear makes perfect sense. Like a beautifully engineered Italian sports car, the Iambic Model T proves performance and luxury can coexist.

#4660. Puerto Rico tapped Sunrun’s home batteries for 18 straight days

Sunrun has doubled participation in its Puerto Rico virtual power plant to more than 60,000 customers, and the grid is putting those home batteries to work: It tapped into them for 18 straight days in October.

A virtual power plant (VPP) connects batteries across thousands of properties and coordinates them to supply power together.

Sunrun says its VPP network in Puerto Rico now includes nearly 70,000 batteries, frequently delivering 45 megawatts (MW) for four hours at a time. It has dispatched them more than 60 times since April, including daily deployments beginning October 13 during unusually hot weather.

For Puerto Ricans, who pay some of the highest electricity prices in the US, getting reliable power for all that money remains a problem. Residential electricity averaged 26.36 cents per kilowatt-hour in August, compared with a US average of 18.16 cents, according to the US Energy Information Administration (EIA).

That makes the batteries already installed at homes pretty useful. The grid can pay to tap their stored energy when supplies get tight, putting existing equipment to work without waiting for a new power plant to be built.

Sunrun’s network grew from around 4,000 customers in 2024 to more than 30,000 in 2025. It says it’s the largest aggregator in Puerto Rico’s Customer Battery Energy Sharing (CBES) program.

LUMA, the island’s grid operator, calls on CBES when it expects electricity demand or reserve needs to exceed available generation. Companies such as Sunrun then manage the battery response automatically.

Homeowners get paid for sharing energy and choose how much to keep for backup. Sunrun says most share a small portion of their total battery capacity; the company earns recurring revenue for operating the network.

Across the wider CBES program, LUMA reported in July that more than 90,000 participating customers had helped provide an average of 75 MW during generation shortfalls.

Puerto Rico’s reliability problem goes well beyond hurricanes.

Customers averaged 36 hours without power in 2025, even excluding major events, according to the US EIA. That’s up 19% from 2024. Mainland US customers generally experience about two hours a year under the same measure. Major events added another 23 hours of outages on the island.

More batteries can help, but the size of the shortfall still matters. In an April regulatory filing, participating aggregators said the program couldn’t prevent every rolling blackout in 2025 because some supply gaps exceeded its roughly 50 MW of four-hour capacity. They’re looking to enroll more batteries so the program can cover larger shortfalls.

#4659. GLP-1s May Help Lower Diabetes, Heart Risks Better Than Standard Prevention

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

GLP-1 drugs are more effective in helping prevent type 2 diabetes than the commonly prescribed medication metformin, according to a new study.

Researchers said GLP-1s such as Ozempic and Mounjaro were more likely to reduce blood sugar to healthy levels in people with prediabetes and obesity.

They added that people prescribed GLP-1 medications had a lower risk of progressing from prediabetes to type 2 diabetes.

The researchers noted that GLP-1 users also had a lower risk of death from any cause as well as fewer heart attacks, strokes, and heart failure events compared with metformin users.

“The great news with prediabetes is that it’s still possible to reverse the progression of the disease,” said Vinicius de Sousa Barzon Serra, MD, a study author and research fellow in cardiovascular medicine at the Mayo Clinic in Scottsdale, Arizona, in a press release. “This research may add to the case for considering GLP-1 medications earlier for certain patients, rather than waiting until they develop type 2 diabetes.”

Serra noted that metformin still remains an effective treatment for people with prediabetes and type 2 diabetes.

“This is less about replacing one medication with another and more about discussing additional options with specific patients,” he said.

The researchers presented their findings at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions 2026 in Chicago. The research has not been published yet in a peer-reviewed journal.

David Cutler, MD, a family medicine physician at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, wasn’t involved in the study, but said the findings were “quite impressive.”

“It elevates the comfort of prescribing GLP-1 drugs as a front-line treatment,” he told Healthline.

Robert Eckel, MD, a former president of the American Heart Association who was likewise not involved in the study, agrees the research provides more options for patients and prescribers.

“GLP-1s provide another option for prevention, perhaps as an add-on therapy. However, costs and access to these medications are important factors,” said Eckel, an endocrinologist at the University of Colorado School of Medicine, in the press release.

For their study, the researchers analyzed the medical records of 256,000 adults in the United States with prediabetes and obesity. About 76% of the subjects were women, and the average age of the participants was 52.

About half of those studied were taking GLP-1 drugs with the active ingredient semaglutide, tirzepatide, liraglutide, or dulaglutide.

The other half had been prescribed metformin, a medication used to help manage blood sugar levels in adults and some children with type 2 diabetes by decreasing glucose production in the liver, reducing glucose absorption from food, and improving the body’s insulin sensitivity.

The researchers reported that the people in the study who were taking GLP-1 drugs had a 1.5 times higher chance of reversing high blood sugar to healthy levels compared to people who were using metformin.

The researchers also noted that GLP-1 medication users had a 31% lower risk of developing type 2 diabetes and a 41% lower risk of death from any cause.

They added that GLP-1 medications were associated with 15% fewer heart attacks, 20% fewer strokes, 25% fewer cases of heart failure, and 8% fewer cases of atrial fibrillation (AFib), a common type of irregular heartbeat.

The researchers cautioned that their study is observational and, therefore, cannot prove a cause-and-effect relationship. They also noted they relied on prescription records, so the frequency and dosage at which patients took their medication was not reflected.

In addition, the GLP-1 drugs were grouped together, so individual differences between medications were not considered.

Eckel said in the news release that the benefits for people taking GLP-1 drugs were probably mainly due to weight loss. Eckel noted that the research results open up a wide range of possibilities.

“This is an important finding because the GLP-1 receptor agonists are commonly used today and this is a population that in the transition from prediabetes to diabetes are at increasing risk for cardiovascular disease,” Eckel said in a taped interview alongside the study findings.

Cutler pointed out that several GLP-1 drugs also target blood sugar levels and insulin production. They could be effective in people with prediabetes who don’t have weight management issues.

Cutler noted that these people, however, might be reluctant to take GLP-1 drugs because they may not be experiencing symptoms of their prediabetes but could develop side effects with the medications.

“They would not be getting any immediate benefits,” Cutler said. He added that metformin, which was first used clinically in 1958, remains an effective alternative. “It’s been proven safe, effective, and it’s very cheap,” Cutler said.

It’s estimated that 40 million people in the United States have diabetes, with more than 90% of those cases being type 2 diabetes, a chronic condition characterized by high blood glucose levels that results from the body’s ineffective response to insulin or insufficient insulin production.

It’s also estimated that 115 million adults in the United States have prediabetes, a condition in which a person has higher-than-normal blood sugar levels but not high enough to be diagnosed as type 2 diabetes.

Around 5–10% of people with prediabetes develop diabetes every year. More broadly, up to 70% of people with prediabetes eventually develop diabetes.

Medication is sometimes prescribed for people with type 2 diabetes and prediabetes. Lifestyle changes can help reverse type 2 diabetes and prediabetes, as well as prevent the progression from prediabetes to type 2 diabetes.

Cutler said the lifestyle changes needed to prevent type 2 diabetes are pretty clear.

“The most important thing for people with prediabetes to know is they should lose weight, reduce their carbs, exercise daily and, if that doesn’t work, then consider medication,” he said.

#4658. Archaeologists crack a shipwreck’s 400-year-old combination lock

Published Nov 4, 2026 3:00 PM EST

Archaeologists have finally cracked the code to the famed Ann Francis shipwreck’s brass combination treasure lock. However, the 16th century relic didn’t open after hours of painstaking trial-and-error. Researchers at Cardiff University and Amgueddfa Cymru, the National Museum of Wales, relied on highly detailed CT scanning equipment to peer inside the mechanical device and learn the code without touching the lock itself.

“It’s not every day you get to solve a 400-year-old mystery,” David Williams, a Cardiff University biomechanics engineer, said in a statement.

The lock’s combination was lost on December 28, 1583, when the merchant ship Ann Francis sailed into a powerful storm during a return voyage from Spain. The exact crew number is unclear, but all of them (around 14 sailors) reportedly drowned after veering off-course and wrecking along the coast of southern Wales. Unfortunately, at least one other death is likely directly tied to the Ann Francis. Archival evidence suggests locals later accused a “detestable woman” named Mother Gabley of being an “execrable witch” and casting the foul weather responsible for the maritime tragedy. While Mother Gabley’s fate remains unknown, she would have almost certainly been hanged under the recently passed “Act Against Conjurations, Enchantments and Witchcrafts” if brought to trial.

The Ann Francis remained missing for 415 years, until metal detectorist Peter Hughes rediscovered the wreckage while surveying southern Wales’ Margam Beach in 1998. Hughes and archaeologists subsequently spent more than 20 years scouring the area for the ship’s remains. By 2017, preservationists had documented over 800 gold and silver coins from Germany, Spain, and Portugal along with artifacts like compasses, ship equipment, and cutlery.

Still, the wreck’s most famous remnant is the brass combination lock still in working condition after four centuries buried in sand. It’s possible the lock was used to guard those coins, or potentially other valuables that didn’t survive exposure to the elements. Regardless, the lock has remained close with no hints to its four-letter combination for hundreds of years.

“Elizabethan combination locks are known in Britain, but this one is in exceptionally good condition and is associated with a dated wreck, making it a unique find and the code a tantalizing mystery to solve,” said Alastair Willis, senior numismatics curator at Amgueddfa Cymru.

Tampering with the delicate lock was out of the question, but Willis and his colleagues knew what to do. Using micro-computed tomography (micro-CT) scanning, they looked inside the device and determined the correct code.

“By creating a detailed 3D image of the internal mechanism, I could see how the notches lined up with the letters and identify the exact combination,” explained Williams, who called the experience “certainly a first” for his team.

The correct four-letter combo? A-N-C-E. But with one longstanding question finally answered, another one has arisen.

“Of course, now we’ve solved it, we are left wondering if the code meant something to its owner,” added Willis.
