#4562. The Scion Brand Returns to America With a 3-Cylinder Kei Truck for the U.S.

The formerly youth-focused brand is becoming Toyota’s new “freedom lab” for pushing the boundaries of mobility.

Scion lived a short life, the victim of bad financial timing and millennial misunderstandings. But its parent company, Toyota, is about to give the brand another go—and its market research appears to be spot-on this time, as the Japanese automaker announces a new three-cylinder Kei truck for the U.S. market.

Officially known as the Scion Kei-01, the new model takes traditional Japanese compactness and adds North American levels of capability. The heart of the Kei-01 is a 660cc three-cylinder engine paired with a continuously variable transmission and proper four-wheel drive with push-button lock-up. At 11 feet long and five feet wide, the Kei truck will be even smaller than a modern Mini Cooper.

The Kei-01 will be right-hand-drive, have a maximum speed of 25 miles per hour, and is intended to comply with federal safety requirements for low-speed vehicles. An easily accessible three-way fold-down cargo bed, a payload capacity of 600 pounds, and an extended cabin design with a raised roofline were included specifically for the North American market. Scion has not revealed power figures for the Kei-01, but Toyota did confirm the Kei truck will be available in the U.S. market.

Initially, the Kei-01 will arrive in the U.S. as part of a fleet vehicle pilot program. Scion said this new Kei truck will be an intentionally low-volume, niche vehicle for specific kinds of fleets; it’s targeting small business owners looking for an affordable urban commercial vehicle, farmers requiring a dependable daily workhorse, and municipalities, universities, and corporate campuses seeking efficient fleet vehicles. Last-mile delivery services and outdoor enthusiasts are also being targeted by Toyota. Fleet sales will route through select Toyota dealerships, and the truck will be produced at Toyota Motor Manufacturing Indiana in the second half of 2027.

However, Toyota says it is open to expanding availability of the bite-sized pickup. “Based on market conditions, customer demand, and operational considerations, Toyota may consider expanding availability to limited retail sales at a later date. Additional information and the broader sales strategy will be shared as plans are finalized,” the carmaker stated.

Two additional Scion concept vehicles were showcased alongside the Kei-01 at Toyota Motor North America events in Ypsilanti Township, Michigan, and Frisco, Texas, on Tuesday, November 10. The Scion SxS Concept takes on off-roading with a side-by-side frame and a high-output turbocharged four-cylinder hybrid powertrain. The off-road-focused model will feature over 300 horsepower, significant suspension articulation, and a nimble footprint; there will even be a Silent Mode that shifts motive power to the electric drivetrain.

Additionally, Scion is showing off the BKE Concept, a new kind of mobility tool for the revived automotive brand. Packing only two wheels, the BKE Concept is a personal mobility scooter made for the great outdoors. Scion didn’t provide any other details about the BKE Concept, but it appears to be a comfortable urban commuter.

Regardless of the ultimate plans of Scion’s new Kei truck and concept vehicles, the return of the fun-loving brand is worth celebrating. Toyota has been razor-focused on car enthusiasts with its Gazoo Racing and off-road-focused models, and Scion offers another opportunity for enthusiast appeal. But instead of focusing on young buyers exclusively, Scion will be a “freedom lab” for Toyota, with a focus on experimentation.

“The future of mobility will not be defined by one vehicle, one technology or one way of thinking,” said Simon Humphries, chief branding officer, head of design, Toyota Motor Corporation. “Scion by Toyota gives us a place to challenge conventional thinking, explore new possibilities and create mobility in new ways. The KEI-01, SxS, and BKE concepts each represent a different possibility—and together, they show what can happen when curiosity leads the way.”

A New York transplant hailing from the Pacific Northwest, Emmet White has a passion for anything that goes: cars, bicycles, planes, and motorcycles. After learning to ride at 17, Emmet worked in the motorcycle industry before joining Autoweek in 2022 and Road & Track in 2024. The woes of alternate side parking have kept his fleet moderate, with a 2014 Volkswagen Jetta GLI and a BMW 318i E30 street parked in his Queens community.

#4561. Liebherr expands excavator range with new, 250-tonne electric model

It takes some seriously heavy equipment to make an ultra-class mining truck look little, but that’s exactly what German equipment giant Liebherr does best, and its newest, 250-tonne production excavator keeps that tradition alive – only this time, it’s electric.

Liebherr began converting its diesel-powered mining excavators to electric in limited numbers back in 2024, and electric power has proven to be effective – moving millions of tons of dirt while saving millions of dollars in fuel and maintenance costs. Now, the company is translating that testing experience into regular production practice with the launch of a new, all-electric machine. Meet the R 9300 G8-E.

Based on the proven R 9300 G8 platform, the new Liebherr R 9300 G8-E packs an 850 kW (~1,140 hp) electric drivetrain designed to IEC standards and supports 6-6.6 kV power supplies. The company says its electric setup offers customers the same hydraulic power and bucket capacity (1.8 tonnes/cubic meter, or ~1.5 short tons/cubic yard) as the diesel version.

All that electric power ships with advanced electronics and operator assistance systems designed to maximize both efficiency and safety while giving mine operators more data to work and plan with. Liebherr describes its take on ADAS thusly:

The R 9300 G8-E comes with Liebherr Power Efficiency – Hydraulic Control as standard, which adapts hydraulic power to suit the machine’s load profile, reducing overall engine load factor. Thanks to its Generation 8 electronic architecture, the R 9300 G8-E is compatible with a range of Liebherr’s IoMine technology products, including its range of excavator Assistance Systems, the semi-autonomous Bucket Filling Assistant, the Skyview vision system as well as the data visualisation tool, Data View. Customers also have the option of installing Liebherr’s autonomous cable reel solution onto the excavator to assist with cable management and support machine mobility on site.

Like its repowered cousins, the big electric excavator does seem to have on-board batteries, but is primarily driven and operated with grid power, reducing charging and re-charging concerns and enabling round-the-clock operations for as long as grid power holds.

Liebherr touts the benefits of new R 9300 G8-E’s quiet, emissions-free running throughout its official announcement, but doesn’t stop there. The company says its EV, which makes do with thousands of fewer moving parts in its drivetrain, can also reduce maintenance requirements and associated operating costs in certain applications and site conditions while improving workplace conditions for the people who work in and around the machine.

Operating electric machinery inside mines must be mindblowingly good. Location is quite fixed, so you can just lay a HV cable to the grid with a spool at the vehicle end for local mobility. No noise, no vibration, no dirty emissions that have to be ventilated out for you not to die, instant torque, massive power and less maintenance on top?

The electric drivetrain also reduces vibration inside the cab, improving operator comfort, limiting fatigue, and potentially contributing to a safer working environment.

#4560. 2027 Kawasaki Jet Skis deliver a supercharged, eye-opening performance

Published Nov 8, 2026 5:21 PM EST

In 1964, then-Pontiac division president John Z. Delorean (yes, that Delorean, of Back to the Future movie car fame) invented the muscle car category by bolting the big-block V8 engine from the company’s full-size cars into its lighter intermediate-sized chassis to create the legendary Pontiac GTO.

Kawasaki has done the same thing for its Jet Skis for the 2027 model year by installing the 310-horsepower supercharged 1.5-liter engine from its bigger Ultra models into the sporty, agile Jet Ski STX hull. The result is a truly eye-opening performance with what the company says is its quickest Jet Ski yet.

Kawasaki established the personal watercraft industry with the 1973 introduction of the 27-horsepower JS400 Jet Ski. Since that time, however, the one-time industry leader has slipped in popularity compared to its rivals in the market.

The company’s 2027 plan to recapture customers includes an embrace of high performance. Kawasaki has rolled out five new models for 2027, but the stars of the show are the high-performance Jet Skis meant to excite customers.

The original Jet Ski employed a smokey 400 cc 2-stroke engine that grew to 800 cc over time. Those early Jet Skis were tricky stand-up models that delivered responsive handling but presented a learning curve that saw newcomers falling off repeatedly as they learned to master the machine.

The solution was the introduction of the more stable sit-down models that traded responsiveness for stability. It was a trade that so many riders were willing to make that eventually Kawasaki phased out the stand-up models entirely.

The industry shifted to cleaner 4-stroke engines in the ‘90s, and 1999 saw the arrival of the 1.5-liter engine based on Kawasaki’s sport motorcycle powerplants in its Jet Skis, packing 150 horsepower. In 2007, the engineering team bolted a supercharger to the same engine, producing 250 horsepower.

Now, thanks to the technology of Eaton’s Twin Vortices System supercharger design (which debuted on the 2009 Chevrolet Corvette ZR1), power has reached 310 horsepower. Packed into the agile STX sit-down hull to create the STX 310 model, the big motor lets riders rip across the water at 65 mph.

This drivetrain employs a 4-into-2-into-1 exhaust with dual water mufflers to minimize backpressure, maximizing the engine’s power and efficiency. The 160-mm jet pump has a three-blade impeller whose blade angles are optimized for peak acceleration and thrust.

Kawasaki let us ride the top-of-the-line STX 310RX, which lists for $20,199. There is a slightly less-well-equipped STX 310R that goes just as fast for $18,799. The test unit featured a 7-inch display panel containing the speedometer, tachometer, supercharger boost level, fuel level, trim setting, power mode setting, and compass. The rear-view camera on the STX lets the rider keep an eye on skiers, wakeboarders, or tube riders behind the watercraft.

We’ve gotten familiar with electronically controlled modes in modern cars, trucks, and motorcycles, and they are also present here in the Jet Ski STX 310RX. They are Smart Learning Operation (SLO), Lower Power Operation (LPO), Middle Power Operation (MPO), and Full Power Operation (FPO).

I started riding in MPO, thinking that would be a good get-acquainted scenario and I was pleasantly surprised at the STX 310’s speed. I guess I shouldn’t have been, considering that it has 310 horsepower. After a bit of that, I switched to FPO, and found the throttle response much touchier and acceleration quicker–perfect for big fun.

MPO limits peak power to 80 percent, while FPO unleashes all 310 horses. LPO makes the throttle response even more sluggish and further restricts maximum power to 60 percent. SLO mode requires a special yellow key and is aimed at true beginners, who, realistically, probably should be learning on something other than this supercharged beast.

Other gadgets include the Launch Control system, which automatically adjusts the jet pump’s trim over the course of an acceleration run, keeping it optimized as the boat’s attitude changes during the run. There’s also a handy one-touch 5-mph cruise control, good for complying with no-wake zones.

Hot-dogging on the STX is a good time, thanks to a hull design that was created for corner carving, without much risk of pitching the rider into orbit mid-corner. There are also some nice practical features, like a Neutral that preserves some degree of steering capability.

Jet Skis have no rudder, relying on thrust from the engine to steer them, so when the throttle is released, or the boat is shifted to neutral, you’d expect it to be adrift. But Kawasaki employs a thrust reverser that lets the STX simultaneously have no forward thrust while also having some steering capacity. That reverser also provides for a Reverse position that lets the ride back the STX.

Reverse is one of the amenities that led to the demise of original-style stand-up Jet Skis, which aren’t suited to such features. Kawasaki tried briefly to revive the format in 2017, but says that its new stand-up 2027 models are Back to the Future to stay this time.

I was pleasantly surprised to find that long-dormant stand-up riding skills were still sufficient for me to take off on the first try without falling.

Kawasaki offers two versions of its classic stand-up model for 2027, the Jet Ski SX-R 160 and SX-X 160. These are powered by 160-hp naturally aspirated versions of the 1.5-liter engine, with the difference between them being that the SX-R has a traditional-style moveable handlebar that starts off lying flat and the rider lifts it as they stand.

The SX-X has a fixed motorcross-style handlebar, giving riders a choice between the two styles. The test model was the SX-X motocrosser. I’d never ridden one like that before, but I found the fixed bar seemed to make it easier to pull myself up as the ski got underway.

However, after falling off, as one does on these things, you have to reach up from the water to reattach your wrist lanyard to the ignition interlock. This is the thing that shuts the ski off when you fall so that it doesn’t leave you behind, and you have to reconnect it to restart the machine.

But with the fixed bar up there pretty high from the water, I was happy to have my 35-inch sleeve length. Someone with more normal-length arms might find it hard to reach the switch while floating in the water alongside.

Just as I’d remembered stand-ups, the SX model is tremendously agile and fun for turns and jumps. And just as I remembered, it is easy to fall off in the process. Once it starts to roll onto its side, adding power might get you to ride out of it, or, as in my case, it might just make you hit the water while going even faster!

It doesn’t matter which handlebar style you prefer because both the SX-X 160 and SX-R 160 are $11,999. Getting one of these would allow you to cultivate some old-school riding skills while taking advantage of some throwback value. That was another key component of the original Pontiac GTO’s muscle car legend, so it is good to see in the Kawasaki showrooms for 2027.

#4559. Lucid teases its cheaper sub-$50,000 Cosmos EV in new video and images

Lucid has released a new teaser video of what looks like the Cosmos, its upcoming sub-$50,000 midsize electric SUV and the car that’s supposed to turn Lucid into a volume automaker.

The clip gives us the clearest look yet at the Cosmos’ lighting, front and rear, after months of camouflaged prototype sightings. But the car itself is still about a year away.

Lucid posted the 1 minute 34 second video on X yesterday. The caption talks about “elevating the experience of movement” and says Lucid can’t wait “to share this feeling with even more people.” It doesn’t name the vehicle, but “even more people” is about as subtle a hint at a cheaper model as you can get.

Two frames from the film show the vehicle at dusk. At the rear, “LUCID” is spelled out in red illuminated letters across the tailgate, flanked by thin red light strips, with a spoiler cutting across the base of the rear glass. Up front, a sculpted LED headlight with a row of vertical segments sweeps across a red body panel.

That rear end matches the Cosmos design Lucid registered with the EU Intellectual Property Office in May, which showed the same spelled-out “LUCID” tailgate and rear-glass spoiler. It also lines up with the thin red light strips on the camouflaged Cosmos prototype spotted on Highway 101 in California last month.

Lucid unveiled its plans for Cosmos and Earth at its first Investor Day in March. Both ride on the new midsize platform and start under $50,000, roughly half the price of the Gravity.

On paper, the Cosmos is impressive. Lucid claims about 300 miles of range from a 69 kWh pack, thanks to efficiency of up to 4.5 mi/kWh, which it says is 10% better than its closest competitor. It also claims 200 miles of range in 14 minutes of charging, and its new Atlas drive unit has 30% fewer parts and costs 37% less than the Zeus unit in the Gravity.

The problem is timing. Production was supposed to start in late 2026. In August, CEO Silvio Napoli pushed the Cosmos to 2027, “most likely the second half.”

That puts it on the same schedule as Rivian’s $45,000 base R2, and well after the Tesla Model Y it was caught testing next to in Arizona back in May.

Lucid needs this car badly. It delivered 3,806 vehicles in Q3, down 7% year-over-year, while building only 2,954 after cutting the second shift at its Arizona factory.

I want Lucid to succeed. Period. I love the Air Pure and would like to get one at some point, but the cost is out of my budget while the tech is more than I want or need.

But I think what impresses me more than anything with Lucid is that they are one of the few who actually speak efficiency. It seems that they actually care about being efficient where companies like GM and others just build vehicles with bigger batteries in order to get more range. So for that, I give Lucid much credit.

The company is building hype a year out. It has nothing else new to sell until the Cosmos arrives, and the company reports Q3 earnings on Monday. They need to remind everyone what they are working toward.

A midsize SUV doing 4.5 mi/kWh would be best in class by a wide margin, and Lucid’s efficiency claims have held up on the Air. If it really lands under $50,000 with 300 miles of range, it’s a very compelling alternative to the Model Y and the R2, which still have room to take over market shares from ICE vehicles.

But Lucid has already slipped this car once; it says its cash lasts “well into 2027,” and the Cosmos is due in the second half of 2027. That’s a tight overlap. I think the Cosmos will be a good car, but can Lucid fund it all the way to customers’ driveways?

#4558. Albatross couple George and Geraldine reunite for the 10th straight year

Published Nov 9, 2026 9:00 AM EST

The Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge near Hawaii has welcomed a special couple: George and Geraldine, two short-tailed albatrosses (Phoebastria albatrus). The birds have officially found each other for nesting season on the Midway Atoll for the 10th straight year in a row.  George was first spotted on October 18, and the pair was reunited by October 22.

Every fall, the remote group of islands becomes a temporary home to the world’s largest albatross colony. Albatrosses are a group of large migratory seabird species, including the wandering albatross (Diomedea exulans), which has the largest wingspan of any current bird species. One Laysan albatross (Phoebastria immutabilis), on the other hand, claims the title of oldest known banded wild bird—the famous Wisdom, who is over 70 years old.

Short-tailed albatrosses (called makalena in Hawaiian) are almost completely white and feature a large pink bill. They can live up to 50 years, and as exemplified by George and Geraldine, are monogamous. They nest on islands and atolls, and the species is listed as endangered by both the United States government and the state of Hawaii. At the turn of the 20th century, feather hunting almost made the species go extinct.

“The vast majority of breeding for short-tailed albatross occurs on remote islands in the western Pacific, including Torishima Island, Japan, which is an active volcano south of Tokyo, and the Senkaku Islands near Taiwan,” according to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS). “Since 2000, biologists at the [Midway Atoll National Wildlife] refuge have used short-tailed albatross decoys and audio playback of the seabird’s calls to attract more of them.”

In fact, George and Geraldine are the only breeding pair of short-tailed albatross on the Midway Atoll, though other members of their species were spotted last season. They were banded as chicks on Torishima Island and first seen together on Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge in 2016. The cute pair brought their first chick into the world during the 2018-2019 breeding season.

“Millions of makalena once used their long wingspans to expertly glide on air currents across the northern Pacific Ocean, from Japan to Alaska and Hawaiʻi,” the FWS writes. “The slowly growing population is estimated at around 10,000 today.”

#4557. Drive with Style: Our Favorite Chronographs & Driving Watches (Mostly) under $1000

Our car experts choose every product we feature. We may earn money from the links on this page.

Whether you’re buying a gift for a car lover or just looking to step up your style, check out our favorite watches and chronographs for drivers.

This story was updated in November 2026 with new products and fresh information.

As a watch enthusiast, I know all too well the dilemma friends, partners, and family members face when trying to buy a watch as a gift. Watch people can be incredibly particular. We obsess over case sizes, movements, bracelet designs, dial layouts, and brand history in the same way car enthusiasts argue over engine codes or wheel specs.

That’s what makes this list different. These aren’t cheap knockoffs or forgettable department-store watches. Instead, they’re enthusiast-focused timepieces that capture the spirit, heritage, and personality that make great watches special, without requiring luxury-watch money.

I’ve rounded up a nice selection of vintage-inspired chronographs, quirky design icons, and motorsport-influenced watches that genuine enthusiasts will appreciate, wear often, and happily give real wrist time to long after the wrapping paper is gone.

The Timex Atelier Chronograph Quartz M1q brings a more considered design approach to an accessible everyday chronograph. Its balanced 40mm stainless-steel case, refined subdial layout, and engraved black dial give it a premium look without feeling overly busy, while a double-curved sapphire crystal adds a welcome touch of durability. A Swiss-made quartz chronograph movement keeps time accurately, without the added cost or maintenance of an automatic, and the tachymeter scale offers a useful nod to traditional motorsport watches. It’s available with either an oil- and chemical-resistant NBR rubber strap or a self-adjusting stainless-steel bracelet, and its 100-meter water resistance makes it practical beyond the watch box.

The PRS 516 features a 42mm case, perforated leather strap, and piston-inspired pushers, all nodding directly to Sixties motorsport, while the Swiss automatic chronograph movement underneath gives it legitimate credibility. Tissot has been tied to racing for decades, and the PRS 516 leans into that heritage without feeling like a costume piece. It’s sporty, tactile, and busy in the best possible way.

The Timex Marlin Neo Classic Chronograph takes one of the brand’s most recognizable vintage designs and gives it a cleaner, more streamlined look. Its compact 40mm brushed stainless-steel case, polished top ring, and curved pushers preserve the Marlin’s mid-century character, while three dial and strap combinations offer slightly different takes on the same retro-inspired design. Details like the domed acrylic crystal, multiscale dial markings, and tachymeter scale give it the feel of a vintage instrument watch without making it overly busy. Inside, a quartz chronograph movement provides accurate, low-maintenance timekeeping and a functional stopwatch, making the Neo Classic a handsome everyday option for anyone drawn to classic watch design.

The Form C feels like the automotive equivalent of a stripped-down Bauhaus sports coupe: clean, lightweight, and engineered with restraint. Its 40mm stainless-steel case wears slim, thanks to Junghans’s minimalist German design language, while the calfskin leather strap keeps things understated and comfortable. A reliable quartz chronograph movement fits the watch’s no-nonsense personality and gives it dead-simple usability. Junghans’s heritage stretches back to 1861, and the Form C channels that legacy into a watch that’s more about precision and proportion than flash.

The Seiko Prospex Speedtimer SSC947 pairs motorsport heritage with modern tech in a 41.4 mm stainless-steel case with brushed and polished finishing. Powered by Seiko’s solar V192 movement, it offers a chronograph, 24-hour subdial, power-reserve indicator, and date display, with a six-month reserve when fully charged. The 947 model is my favorite version of the Speedtimer, with its awesome yellow dial. Protected by a curved sapphire crystal with inner antireflective coating and mounted on a three-link stainless bracelet, it’s water-resistant to 100 meters. Seiko’s reputation as a favorite among horologists speaks to the brand’s consistent quality, innovation, and mechanical mastery, making the SSC947 a reliable and stylish choice for both collectors and racing enthusiasts alike.

If the yellow dial is a bit too bold, you can also check out the SSC943 in Ivory and Green, and the panda-dialed SSC813.

Nicknamed the “Bullhead,” the Tsuno Chronograph wears its motorsport inspiration proudly, with its pushers mounted at the top of the 45mm case like vintage rally timers. Citizen revived the design from the brand’s iconic Seventies Bullhead chronographs, combining retro styling with modern Eco-Drive solar-powered quartz tech that eliminates battery changes. It’s bold, unapologetically funky, and one of the most distinctive modern chronographs you can buy without crossing into luxury-watch pricing.

Featuring a 41mm stainless-steel case with brushed and polished surfaces, this Alpina Startimer is powered by a quartz chronograph movement. A large “Big Date” window sits at 6 o’clock, and a 100-meter water-resistance rating ensures a bit of water won’t be a worry. The white dial sports bold numerals, luminous hands, and a red-triangle chronograph seconds hand, and it is protected by a scratch-resistant sapphire crystal. It comes with a three-link stainless-steel bracelet and delivers chronograph utility in a clean, sporty package.

The Conquest Chronograph features a 42mm stainless-steel case, ceramic tachymeter bezel, and automatic chronograph movement, striking an excellent balance between luxury and sportiness. Longines has deep roots in timing motorsport and aviation events dating back over a century, and the Conquest channels that pedigree into a polished, well-rounded package.

The Bulova Racer 150th Anniversary Shelby pairs motorsport style with serious precision. Powered by Precisionist movement, it delivers exceptional accuracy and a smooth sweeping second hand, plus a 1/1000-second chronograph for track-ready performance. The bold blue dial, sapphire crystal, and 43mm stainless-steel case channel classic racing design, while the lightweight striped rubber strap keeps it comfortable for everyday wear. Rugged, refined, and collector-worthy, this limited-edition timepiece is engineered to stand out.

The Bulova Racer Chronograph stands out thanks to its sharp case lines, bold subdials, and an aggressive motorsport-inspired aesthetic. Its stainless-steel case measures around 42mm and pairs with a sporty bracelet setup, while the quartz chronograph movement emphasizes precision and practicality. Bulova’s long history in American watchmaking, including timing innovations and racing partnerships, gives the Racer more authenticity than its flashy styling initially suggests.

The Legacy Tonneau Chronograph has a distinctly Seventies flavor, with its curved rectangular case shape and integrated-bracelet-inspired design evoking vintage sports watches of the era. Timex keeps things simple with a quartz chronograph movement and stainless-steel construction that prioritizes durability and affordability over pretense. The tonneau-shaped case wears differently from traditional round chronographs, giving it a cool retro personality. It’s proof that enthusiast-oriented design doesn’t have to come with a luxury-watch price tag

The Citizen Eco-Drive Weekender Brycen Chronograph is a sharp, 44 mm watch with a bold blue dial that looks great on the wrist. It’s powered by light, so you never need to change a battery, and it packs a chronograph, 12/24‑hour time, a date window, and 100-meter water resistance. Stylish, tough, and low-maintenance, it’s perfect for everyday wear or weekend adventures.

The Ventura Chrono is pure mid-century Americana. Its asymmetrical 32.3mm-by-50.3mm triangular case design became iconic after Elvis Presley famously wore one, and Hamilton has kept the look alive with modern chronograph hardware and a supple leather strap. Powered by a quartz chronograph movement, the Ventura trades traditional racing-watch cues for style and wrist presence. It’s like a Sixties concept car brought to life.

The Swatch New Chrono takes a lighthearted approach to a chronograph, with a 43mm stainless‑steel case, intuitive chronograph subdials, a tachymeter bezel, and a reliable Swiss quartz movement. Whether you’re timing sprint starts or simply want a watch that looks dynamic on your wrist, this piece combines accessible build quality, youthful design cues, and a distinctive racing-inspired spirit.

This iconic watch retains the classic Marlin Sixties design features that make it so cool and timeless. With a domed acrylic crystal lens and retro-style square markers at 3, 9, and 12 o'clock, it features a natural leather strap and a tachymeter index along its outer minute track to measure speed. We dig the racing stripes on this blue version, but many face and band combinations are available.

Built for serious outdoor missions, this timepiece features a rugged 45mm Carbonox case, unidirectional bezel, and 300-meter water resistance, ready for land, sea, or whatever the trail throws at you. With 18 tritium light tubes that ensure visibility for up to 25 years, an orange screw-in crown, and the “Never Give Up” motto engraved on the caseback alongside Bear Grylls’s signature, it combines Swiss precision with no-compromise practicality.

Featuring a distinctive square resin case, the AE1200WHD‑1A is a retro‑futuristic digital watch built for function and value. It offers world time across 31 time zones (48 cities + UTC), a 1/100‑second stopwatch, a countdown timer, five daily alarms, and a full auto‑calendar up to 2099. With an impressively long 10‑year battery life, 100-meter water resistance, LED backlight, and a stainless‑steel bracelet, it is the perfect beater watch for a seasoned horologist or a gateway drug to the uninitiated.

The Timex Q Chronograph blends vintage charm with modern functionality in a stainless-steel 38mm case that channels late-Seventies sports-watch aesthetics. Powered by a quartz chronograph movement, it features a day-date window, a rotating bezel, and subtle retro accents such as a distressed leather strap.

#4556. Tesla hikes Cybertruck prices up to 10% after announcing it will kill production

Tesla has raised Cybertruck prices in the US by up to 10% and stopped taking orders for the base Dual Motor AWD trim. The cheapest Cybertruck you can actually order now costs $92,490.

The move comes right after Tesla confirmed it will end Cybertruck production at Gigafactory Texas around mid-2027.

Here’s what Tesla’s online configurator shows today, compared to the prices set in August:

The Dual Motor trim still shows a new, higher price on Tesla’s website, but the option is greyed out. So Tesla raised the price of a version it isn’t selling anymore.

This is the second price hike in less than three months. Tesla raised prices by $5,000 on two trims in August, when the Dual Motor went from $69,990 to $74,990 and the Premium AWD from $79,990 to $84,990.

Add it up and the Premium AWD is now $12,500 (15.6%) more expensive than it was in early August. And the entry price for any Cybertruck you can order went from $69,990 to $92,490. That’s a 32% jump in about 10 weeks.

For reference, Tesla unveiled the Cybertruck in 2019 with a promised starting price of $39,900.

The price hikes make little sense from a demand standpoint. Tesla doesn’t break out Cybertruck deliveries, but its “Other Models” category, which also includes the Model S, Model X, and Semi, fell 48% year-over-year to 8,295 units in Q3. We estimate Cybertrucks made up 7,000 to 8,000 of those, about 12% of the line’s 250,000-unit annual capacity.

Tesla also tried the opposite approach earlier this year. It offered a dual-motor Cybertruck at $59,990 in February for “only the next 10 days,” then pulled it. A single-motor RWD version was discontinued after just 173 sales. None of it moved the needle.

The Cybertruck isn’t sold in Europe or most right-hand-drive markets, and Tesla canceled it for Australia and New Zealand last month.

So, Tesla has now discontinued more models than it currently offers. Looks like the great leader isn’t particularly good at writing product specs. And the hype has been over for quite a while anyway. In Europe, owning a Tesla has actually become something of an image liability.

This is what a wind-down looks like. Tesla isn’t trying to sell more Cybertrucks anymore. It’s trying to make as much money as possible on the last ones, with the hope that announcing the end of production will encourage some people to secure their order.

Once you’ve decided to end a program, volume stops mattering. You have a set number of build slots left, a parts supply you want to burn down, and probably a small group of fans who’ll want one before it’s gone. Pausing the cheapest trim and charging $7,500 more for the rest is the obvious play. You push everyone into higher-margin configurations and stop pretending the base truck is a real product.

But it does say a lot about the last two years of Cybertruck pricing. Tesla went from a $59,990 “limited-time” offer in February to a $92,490 entry price in November. That’s a company that never figured out who the truck was for.

#4555. Voyager 1 is almost one light-day away from Earth

Published Nov 9, 2026 10:00 AM EST

Voyager 1, the NASA space probe that has traveled farther from Earth than any other human-made object, is closing in on a remarkable milestone. Actually, let’s call it a 16.09-billion-milestone. That’s the distance a photon can travel in a single day, which is to say the Voyager 1 spacecraft will be exactly one light-day away from our planet on November 18 at 5:18 a.m. EST.

At that moment, a radio signal sent from Earth would take 24 hours to reach Voyager 1, and then it would take another 24 hours for the probe’s response to come back. Imagine on a Friday morning telling your oven to turn on, but you don’t receive confirmation that it’s hot until Sunday. And by that point, the oven would have been baking whatever was inside for most of Saturday. That is the kind of delay that NASA’s Voyager team must work with.

Communicating with a machine at this superlative distance is “a pretty incredible endeavor,” Princeton University research scientist and heliophysicist Jamie S. Rankin tells Popular Science. Rankin is also a deputy project scientist of the Voyager mission. “In my mind the fun is receiving a signal back from the Voyager, a light-day away.”

Rankin and other astronomers use those signals to study the very local interstellar medium, which is the suburb of space surrounding our solar system. Voyager 1 has been in this region, about 11 billion miles away, since 2012. There, the probe can detect changes in plasma and the magnetic field.

“Right now we’re trying to figure out how far out are the influences of the sun felt,” she says.

The sun continuously spits out charged particles in a stream of solar wind that extends into space. That wind pushes back against the gas and other interstellar stuff surrounding our solar system, sculpting a bubble in space known as the heliosphere. “There will be some part farther out, some distance away [where the] interstellar medium has no idea that the heliosphere is even there,” she says. Rankin adds that she thinks Voyager 1 is right on the edge of this “undisturbed, pristine interstellar medium.”

It is something of a marvel that the almost 50-year-old Voyager 1 continues to supply astronomers with data. To send information to Earth, the probe uses a 23-watt radio transmitter (about the output of a small refrigerator lightbulb). Only antennas as sensitive as the 70-meter-wide dishes in the NASA Deep Space Network can detect Voyager 1’s super-faint signal. Without them, the space probe would have gone incommunicado years ago.

When Voyager 1 launched in September 1977, the nuclear-powered spacecraft had 10 operational scientific instruments. It discovered new moons orbiting Jupiter and Saturn on its way out of our solar system; its observations of Jupiter’s moon Europa hinted at a liquid ocean under an icy crust. When the probe traveled beyond our solar system’s planets, NASA’s Voyager team shut down unnecessary equipment to conserve power. Now only two of its instruments are active. Ongoing management continues to preserve as much juice as possible from the spacecraft’s dwindling plutonium supply. The team was also forced to turn off the Low-energy Charged Particles experiment in April. In September, NASA swapped out three systems for lower-power alternatives on the Voyager 1, about six weeks after the same strategy worked on its twin Voyager 2 probe.

“It’s fun to see what sort of innovation people come up with to keep the spacecraft going,” Rankin says. “There’s only so much you can turn off.”

Voyagers 1 and 2 have been operating without several instrument heaters for years. If shutting those off hadn’t worked, Rankin says “the mission would have ended a decade ago.”

Still, its operational margins are thin. In late October, NASA briefly lost contact with Voyager 1; that issue has appeared to resolve itself and may have been related to a group of thrusters going offline.

“This is the first time we’ve seen the spacecraft do something like this, but we are also at a point in the mission where we have to expect the unexpected,” Kareem Badaruddin, Voyager mission manager at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), said in a news release. “We’re relieved to be back in contact with Voyager 1 and are eager to understand what happened.” (JPL representatives did not respond to Popular Science’s requests for comment.)

All spacecraft missions must come to an end, no matter how plucky the probe or innovative its engineering team. NASA estimates that the Deep Space Network will lose contact with Voyager 1 around 2036, long before it travels to its two-light-day milestone. The probe may also freeze, unable to point properly back at Earth. Or its power systems will finally go kaput.

“We know that’s coming at some point. It’s probably not 20 years from now,” Rankin says. “It’s probably not 10 years from now.”

And then Voyager 1 will go forever radio silent as it cruises onward through the heavens.

#4554. Kia’s PV7 electric van stretches over 17 feet and seats 9

Kia is expanding its electric van lineup with the PV7, a larger PV5 sibling that can carry nine people or a whole lot of cargo.

The PV5, Kia’s first fully electric van from its Platform Beyond Vehicle (PBV) business, is proving to be a bigger hit than expected.

A year after it went on sale, the PV5 quickly became Europe’s most popular small electric van. In the first half of 2026, it was the top seller in its segment, accounting for 37% of electric C-segment van sales across Europe.

Next year, Kia will launch the PV7, the second electric van from its PBV business. Kia revealed the PV7 at IAA Transportation in Hanover, Germany, in September.

It’s based on the same E-GMP.S platform as the PV5, but the PV7 features a considerably longer wheelbase and stretched body, opening up more space inside.

The PV7 is over 17.5 ft long, measuring 5,350 mm long, 1,995 mm wide, and 1,990 mm high, with a 3,500 mm wheelbase. In comparison, the PV5 is just 4,695 mm long, 1,895 mm wide, and 1,915 mm tall, with a 2,995 mm wheelbase.

That’s even bigger than the Volkswagen ID. Buzz Long-Wheelbase (LWB), which measures 4,962 mm in length with a 3,239 mm wheelbase.

Like the PV5, the PV7 will initially be available in Passenger and Cargo body styles, but Kia plans to launch 23 different variants, or “top hats,” over the next few years.

It will be offered with two nickel-cobalt-manganese (NCM) battery packs: 71.5 kWh and 96.2 kWh. The Long Range Cargo model offers an all-electric WLTP range of over 460 km (285 miles). Even at full capacity, Kia said the new PV7 achieves nearly 400 km (248 miles) of range and still has 350 liters of trunk space.

A plena capacidad la nueva #PV7 consigue casi 400 km de autonomía y aún reserva 350 litros de maletero #Kia #KiaPV7 #MovementThatInspires pic.twitter.com/fzIvviYZuE

Front-wheel drive (FWD) will be standard at launch, but Kia plans to add an all-wheel drive (AWD) option later.

Depending on the configuration, the FWD electric powertrain delivers up to 268 horsepower (200 kW) and 309 lb-ft (420 Nm) of torque.

Thanks to its 800V architecture, the Kia PV7’s battery can charge from 10% to 80% in about 25 minutes with a 350 kW DC fast charger. It will be Kia’s first vehicle with two charging ports, including a front AC/DC port and an optional rear side AC port.

With vehicle-to-load (V2L) capabilities, it can serve as a mobile power source for tools, equipment, a campsite, or other external electronic devices.

The PV7 Cargo, designed for businesses, fleets, and logistics, is available in 2- and 3-seat configurations and offers up to 6.1 cubic meters of cargo space. The High Roof variant offers even more, with up to 8 cubic meters.

Maximum payload is up to 1,165 kg (2,568 lbs) for the Cargo Long and up to 1,200 kg (2,645 lbs) for the compact model.

The PV7 Cargo Long features a 550 mm loading height and, according to Kia, enough capacity for up to three Euro pallets (800 x 1,200 mm). An added heavy-duty mode adjusts the vehicle’s response to varying payloads to help maintain stability and control while driving.

Depending on the use, buyers can choose between full-open twin-swing tailgate doors or a lift-up tailgate.

The PV7 Passenger, on the other hand, is designed for personal use and families, or can also be used as a shuttle with room for up to nine passengers in the global version. In Korea, it will seat up to 11 passengers.

The 7-seater features Long-Rail Easy Remove Seats, enabling various interior seating configurations. The 9-seater variant, on the other hand, is available with or without a fourth row.

Inside, both versions feature Hyundai’s new Pleos Connect infotainment system, with 12.9″ and 14.6″ display screens and physical controls for commonly used functions.

The system runs Android Automotive OS, making it more like a smartphone with apps and customizable screens. It also includes Hyundai’s Gleo AI, an AI-powered in-car companion that can answer questions, control navigation or vehicle functions, and more.

Nice vehicle but once again Kia/Hyundai short changes on battery capacity. A 138" (3500 mm) wheelbase means plenty of room for a 140-150kwh battery (BMW and Rivian do that with vastly less space). That would give it a proper EPA range of over 300 miles with passengers or cargo. Instead this will be in the low 200s unloaded and 170-190 IRL. Offer it as a $7k upgrade. smh

Kia said the PV7 is based on a “Mobile Workspace” concept, with a layered dashboard and center console to optimize space.

The Kia PV7 Passenger and Cargo will go on sale in Korea and Europe in the second half of 2027. It will then roll out to new markets with new derivatives and conversions.

Kia will announce PV7 prices closer to its launch. In Korea, the PV5 Passenger and Cargo Compact starts at 45.9 million won ($34,000) and 41 million won ($30,000), respectively. In Germany, the PV5 Passenger 5-seater starts at €38,690 ($43,000).

#4553. Fake rocks boost survival for venomous Australian snakes

Published Nov 9, 2026 11:48 AM EST

Australia’s broad-headed snake (Hoplocephalus bungaroides) is as unique as it is threatened. However, ecologists at the University of Technology Sydney (UTS) have good news about this reptile. According to researchers, four of six captive-bred juveniles recently released into the Australian bush have survived their initial, most dangerous months outdoors. The team’s first-of-its-kind program may provide a promising path forward for the species—and a set of bespoke, artificial rocks may be the key.

“Reintroducing any threatened species is challenging, especially when they’re captive bred,” explained University of Technology Sydney (UTS) wildlife ecologist Jonathan Webb. “When the juvenile snakes are released, they risk getting eaten by either native predators, like kookaburras and brown snakes, or invasive predators such as cats or foxes.”

The broad-headed snake’s current predicament is the result of multiple issues. The distinct, yellow-banded serpent is slow to mature, and only begins reproducing around five years old. When it does, the nearly three-foot-long snake is one of the only venomous species known to give birth to live offspring. Although adults can live as long as 23 years in their native Sydney Basin, females only mate every two or three years. This leaves the broad-headed snake extremely susceptible to climate change, human impacts, and invasive predators. Any disruptions to the reproductive cycle can destabilize Australia’s population for generations—and the species has experienced plenty of disruptions over the last few decades.

“The broad-headed snake fascinated me because it used to be very common in the Sydney region, but even in the 1990’s it was quite rare,” said Webb. “Why was this species in trouble when other snake species were doing okay?”

Webb noted that Australia’s increasingly frequent droughts and wildfires, coupled with habitat destruction, have made the broad-headed snake one the continent’s most threatened species. The intentional removal of bush-rocks for landscaping projects is also rough on the animals.Juveniles are particularly hard hit, as they rely on the bush-rocks for shelter and a steady diet of other reptiles like skinks and geckos.

“You can still buy rocks and boulders taken from the bush at your local landscape supplier, which is something I find really frustrating,” said Webb, adding that a single attractive boulder can sell for as much as $450. “That’s a pretty strong incentive for people.”

In collaboration with the conservation organization Aussie Ark and Indigenous representatives of the Traditional Owners of the Shoalhaven region, Webb’s team have bred eight broad-headed snakes in captivity since 2024. Biologists kept one pair of snakes for their genetics, then released the other six at restoration sites in May. However, the juveniles weren’t left stranded in the bush. Researchers placed them beneath custom artificial rocks designed with ideal crevice measurements to mirror natural geologic formations’ thermal properties. Webb said the rocks were “critical” to the snakes’ survival odds.

“Broad-headed snakes are nocturnal so they shelter under these rocks during the day and rely on them for warmth, protection and to attract prey,” he explained.

Biologists hope to expand the program elsewhere in Australia, and breed even more broad-headed snakes for release. Although it’s a slow process, their early successes indicate a potentially ecosystem-altering solution for the reptiles.

“We now have a unique, multi-faceted, holistic program that’s a model for threatened species conservation Australia-wide, and I couldn’t be prouder of our team and our partners,” added Aussie Ark founder Tim Faulkner.

#4552. Hungarian VW Bus Goes from ‘Matchbox: The Movie’ to Matchbox, the Toy Car

A 1976 Volkswagen T2 achieves fame and immortality.

Filmed in Budapest and Bratislava, Matchbox: The Movie has a fairly tenuous connection to the little die-cast toys. Starring the always charismatic John Cena as a CIA agent racing to deal with a rogue nuclear weapon, the central conceit is that a group of friends who used to play together with Matchbox cars in middle school reunite in adulthood to take down the bad guys.

It’s a movie that plays like a kid narrating a story while pushing die-cast cars around the carpet, which feels like a pretty good fit for the brand association. Compared to Hot Wheels, which are all about speed and pulling off loops on those iconic orange tracks, Matchbox as a brand skews a little more realistic, and often features construction machines and vintage vehicles.

See all results for used cars for sale near 97229

Speaking of iconic orange, one of the central vehicles onscreen is a 1970s Volkswagen T2, the beloved Microbus. These things are such a huge part of popular culture that one was the main plot point in an episode of Futurama, which saw the crew hopping into a VW Bus and following Beck’s band around. (Best joke: When asked by Professor Farnsworth where the onboard time dilation device is, Fry reaches under the seat and produces a bong.)

In this case, two VW T2s were used in filming, both owned by Budapest-based Dávid Sipos. One of the two needed sufficient modification for stunt driving that it ended up no longer road legal, but the more original of the pair survived the filming schedule unscathed and came back into Sipos’s possession. As a tie-in with the film, Mattel of course produced Matchbox models of the film cars, and Sipos was delighted to find that the blister-pack model of the VW Bus was a faithful match for his car, right down to the aftermarket sunroof and identical Hungarian license plate.

The story gets even better, with the involvement of the original owner who picked up the keys to this orange bus some 50 years ago. If a VW Microbus is a symbol of counterculture in the U.S., that’s not the case overseas. In 1964, reacting to European tariffs on U.S. chicken products, President Lyndon B. Johnson enacted the so-called “chicken tax,” slapping a 25 percent penalty on various products including imported European light trucks.

For Volkswagen, this meant the death knell of U.S.-exported T2 pickups and panel vans, so the Microbus was typically a passenger van stateside. In Europe, working T2s continued chugging along as part of the furniture of a busy city, getting people and goods where they needed to go.

See all results for used cars for sale near 97229

This particular 1976 T2B was delivered by train to Budapest for the Hungarian Water Works to use as a service vehicle. A young employee with the last name Thaly drove it right off the rail car at the depot, and it entered fleet service for the next eight years.

By 1984, something more modern was needed, so the company offered the VW to Thaly, who promptly snapped it up. He kept working, but the T2 effectively enjoyed a sunny retirement, stored carefully in a garage and used as a summertime camping vehicle driven throughout Europe, first with his children, then with his grandchildren. This went on for three decades.

In more recent times, Sipos was working for an advertising agency that often landed accounts for youth-oriented brands. “Somehow I was always the one suggesting that we should have a VW Bus covered in the brand’s graphics as part of the campaign,” he says.

The company eventually bought a slightly earlier 1972 T2A for permanent use as a rolling billboard. Far from just being a work vehicle, employees started borrowing it outside work and just driving it around, as the experience was so much fun.

“There’s something about traveling in a VW Bus that instantly creates a sense of community,” Sipos says.

The T2 became something of a signature of the agency, with friends and colleagues often flagging likely-looking vehicles up for sale. One day in 2013, Thaly’s beloved orange VW cropped up in a listing, and while the advertising company didn’t need it in the fleet, Sipos bought it as a personal vehicle.

This T2 ended up onscreen when Matchbox's director, Sam Hargrave, spotted a photo of it. Sipos also had a second, very similar T2 at the time, green in color, and it was the latter that was cloned to look like the 1976 T2B and modified for stunt work.

The story of how the actual Hungarian registration ended up on the toy car is a bit of a mystery, as the onscreen cars used different license plates. Mattel’s designers would have had piles of reference photos to comb through, and somehow it was settled that the detail on the plate would be DJN-623, the plate this van has been wearing since 1993.

Sipos made sure to get this unexpectedly accurate model of the Thaly family’s beloved orange Volkswagen to them, and he keeps in close contact with them. How typical of a Volkswagen Bus to still be bringing people together, 50 years after it hit the road.

#4551. The BMW iX3 smashed its EPA range rating, driving well over 400 miles in a real-world test

BMW’s new iX3 outperformed the Volvo EX60 and Mercedes-Benz GLC EV, driving well over 400 miles during a real-world range test.

In a recent nationally representative survey, BMW found that Americans want more EV range than they actually need.

The study found that 73% consider 75 miles of range, or less, enough to cover their daily driving. Meanwhile, 42% said they would require at least 300 miles of range to consider an EV.

Another 53% said they would be more likely to consider an EV if it could add about 150 miles of range in 10 minutes.

BMW’s new iX3 checks all the boxes. Based on BMW’s sixth-generation (Gen6) eDrive 800V system, the 2027 iX3 50 xDrive delivers an EPA-estimated range of up to 434 miles (with 20″ summer tires).

With the 22″ summer tires, the iX3 50 xDrive has an EPA-estimated range of up to 392 miles. Still, plenty for at least a week of commuting.

It can also add 170-185 miles of range in 10 minutes with up to 400 kW DC fast charging. In everyday, real-world driving, it may drive even further than its official EPA numbers suggest.

During Edmunds‘ EV Range test, the 2027 BMW iX3 50 xDrive (with 22″ summer tires) drove 436 miles on a single charge, topping its EPA estimate of 392 miles by 44 miles.

The electric SUV was also more efficient than advertised. The iX3 achieved an energy consumption of 28.3 kWh per 100 miles, beating its EPA estimate of 32 kWh per 100 miles by roughly 11.6%.

BMW’s new iX3 is now the longest-range luxury electric SUV that Edmunds has tested, outperforming rivals including the 2027 Volvo EX60 (352 miles) and Mercedes-Benz GLC Electric (392 miles).

The Edmunds real-world range test is designed to provide a more accurate estimate of an EV’s range in everyday driving conditions.

It consists of 60% city and 40% highway driving with an average speed of 40 mph. The vehicle stays within 5 mph of the posted speed limit, and the climate control is set to auto at 72 degrees.

The 2027 BMW iX3 50 xDrive is available to order in Sport, M Sport, and M Sport Professional trims, priced from $61,500, $64,000, and $65,500, respectively.

Average speed of 40 mph in perfect weather is an absolute best case scenario for EVs. I think cold weather 70 mph would be the worst case and it should be tested.

That said, I think BMW and Mercedes tend to underrate their cars published range (I think they publish worst case condition range). BMW iX and Mercedes have historically outperformed EPA ratings according to various articles and reddits posts.

But I think regardless of what we think of Edmunds tests, these are some crazy range figures and with roughly 100kwh usable battery capacity, you are still looking at close to 4 miles per kwh. As an example across the Ultium platform anything from Chevy or Cadillac barely breaches 300 miles. The big Escalade and pickup trucks have 225+ kwh battery so I am not counting them.

If the depreciation rate for luxury EVs holds up, in 2-3 years, they will be awesome value.

Powered by a 108.7 kWh battery, the new iX3 with 20″ Summer Tires delivers up to 434 miles of range on a single charge.

With a charging rate of up to 400 kW, the new BMW iX3 can recharge from 10% to 80% in about 21 minutes, or add about 185 miles in 10 minutes.

Inside, the electric SUV features the Neue Klasse interior design. The setup includes BMW’s new Panoramic Vision, a full-length windshield display, and a 17.9″ central infotainment screen running the latest Operating System X. Buyers can also upgrade to the optional BMW 3D Head-Up Display.

#4550. Bald eagle Shadow defends Kaydee and his nest from intruder

Published Nov 9, 2026 12:54 PM EST

Word to the wise: don’t mess with Shadow’s nest. For the first time in two weeks, the internet-famous bald eagle’s (Haliaeetus leucocephalus) vocals were heard on the camera that captures a 24/7 livestream of his nest in Southern California. Shadow’s potentially new partner Kaydee was also heard nearby and she landed on the nest.

However, just after landing, Kaydee was on high alert because another eagle was eyeing the nest from above. Shadow quickly responded with loud vocals, and came swooping past the nest. While the intruding eagle briefly followed Shadow away, it made a turn back towards the nest. Kaydee made more calls to Shadow and quickly flew out of the nest, as the intruder tried to land on the branches above her. Shadow returned to the nest, and put himself between Kaydee and the intruder above, and all three birds flew away. Eventually, Shadow perched on a nearby tree and was heard giving a warning call in a loud voice while standing watch. The scene that appeared straight out of a movie was another exciting moment for the eagles of Big Bear Valley.

“The brief encounter last night definitely showed Shadow and Kaydee defending the nest, protecting it and each other,” writes Friends of Big Bear Valley (FOBBV), the non-profit organization that runs the livestream. “What a delight to see them as they have truly been missed these past two weeks!”

According to FOBBV, Shadow is ALSO an “experienced master builder and knows exactly when it’s time to begin tidying up the nest, moving stick furniture or placing new guardrails or a baby gate.”

We still do not know if Shadow and Kaydee will mate this season. Bald eagle nesting officially begins in September, and lasts over six months, depending on when the the chicks fledge. Eggs are typically laid in January.  Viewers can follow Shadow and Kaydee and their journey on the nest via a 24/7 livestream.

Kaydee, formerly known as KD1, is a banded female bald eagle that has been spotted in Big Bear Valley following the death of Shadow’s former partner, Jackie. She was born in 2022, about 70 miles away from Big Bear Lake in the Prado Basin between Anaheim and Riverside, California. Coincidentally, her parents are also named Lucky and Ricky like Jackie’s parents, but they are a different eagle pair.

Kaydee was banded as part of the Orange County Water District’s work to track the eagles born in the area. These bands help biologists track and monitor the birds over time. Kaydee currently has a black spot on her head, but it may not be permanent. It’s possible that not all of her white feathers have come in or it could be tree sap or dirt. She also has two small bands on her legs. One is a small metal band, while the other is a lavender band with “KD1” on it.

Kaydee is almost five years old, so she is just about ready to mate. She was recently spotted on FOBBV’s livestream inspecting the nest and has also been seen hanging out near Shadow. Flying around Big Bear is completely normal behavior for young adult eagles at this time of year.

In January, Jackie laid two eggs in the nest, but ravens destroyed them. She later laid two more eggs that hatched in April and named Luna and Sandy. The name Sandy is in honor of FOBBV’s former executive director Sandy Steers who died from cancer in February.

On July 17, Jackie was found injured on the ground near Dana Point Park, California. Cell phone video from a witness confirmed that she had an altercation with two other subadult eagles. She successfully fended off the other eagles by turning over and using her talons, but could not fly far away.

She was transferred to the Ojai Raptor Center for care, where she was diagnosed with severe anemia. Her anemia worsened during the first week of August, the Ojai Raptor Center said that she was in unstable condition on August 9. Her packed cell volume (PCV) fell below percent, before rising to nine percent. Jackie died early in the morning on August 10. The necropsy did not reveal a single cause of death, and instead pointed to several factors including severe anemia, bird flu, blood clots in her wing and one kidney, and liver and lung abnormalities.

A memorial service was held on September 5 in Fawnskin, California, along with a second celebration of life called Wings Over Big Bear on October 3. The event featured representatives from FOBBV, the Yuhaaviatam of San Manuel Nation, and more.

#4549. Ezra Dyer: Maybe the Saturn Sky Red Line Is Not Quite a Discount Viper, but It Comes Close

This car is proof that the old GM’s ideas weren’t all bad, as I find out when I take custody of one.

From the November/December 2026 issue of Car and Driver.

Back in 2007, I gave my father-in-law, Roger, a ride in a Dodge Viper test car. He loved it, and I offhandedly said, “If you like this, a Saturn Sky Red Line is 80 percent of the performance for 30 percent of the price.” That was the extent of my salesmanship, so I was surprised a month or so later to learn that he’d gone out and bought a new Sky Red Line—for less than $30,000.

I mean, people ask me for car-buying advice all the time. But the way it usually works is that someone asks my pick for an electric sedan, I tell them to drive a Lucid Air, and then they buy an F-350 Power Stroke. So Roger’s follow-through was both rewarding and unnerving, because now he owned a Sky, and I owned my opinion, which is dangerous. I once had a boss who asked me to name a car that was “overpowered but understated,” and I blurted three words that I came to regret: “Volkswagen Phaeton W-12.” I think soon thereafter the company handbook was amended to make Phaeton recommendations a fireable HR violation.

See all results for used cars for sale near 20147

Fortunately, Roger liked the Sky, the first new GM car he’d purchased since a 1982 Camaro Berlinetta that was so terrible that he swore he’d never buy another GM vehicle. He usually sticks to such decrees, but maybe Saturn got a pass because the brand wasn’t around when his Chevy was putting him on a first-name basis with the local tow-truck dispatchers. In any case, the only problem the Sky ever had pertained to the notorious GM ignition-switch recall, wherein pre-bankruptcy GM’s pathological commitment to cheapness led to ignition cylinders unfit for a Little Tikes Cozy Coupe and thus occasional random engine shutdowns. This happened to Roger once on a back road, but he was unbothered. “I just put it in neutral, restarted it, and kept driving,” he told me. “Didn’t even stop.” I guess the Camaro might have permanently recalibrated his expectations for build quality.

Eventually, Roger stopped driving, but he still liked the Sky, so it sat in his driveway long enough for the neighbors to plant hedges so they wouldn’t have to look at it. But where they saw a dented, pollen-crusted car with two flat tires, I saw a dented, pollen-crusted car with two flat tires and a 260-hp turbo four, a stick shift, rear-wheel drive, and a limited-slip differential. Roger said that if I could get it going, I could have it for the bargain price of “get it out of my driveway.”

So, one day, I arrived with a battery jump pack, an air compressor, and five gallons of fresh gas. The questionable tires held air, and the electrics powered up. I splashed in some fuel and turned the key. The Sky fired up like it had been parked an hour before, its digital odometer showing just 43,000 miles. I put it in neutral, let out the clutch, and it immediately stalled because it wasn’t actually in neutral. Turns out you can wiggle the Red Line shifter side to side quite a bit even when it’s in second gear.

See all results for used cars for sale near 20147

Other revelations mostly pertained to ran-when-parked status. The flat-spotted tires and various wheel-on-curb encounters gave the Sky the ride and directional stability of a grocery cart you pull out of the corral and immediately swap for a different one. The battery wouldn’t hold a charge, the interior smelled like a cologne called Old Must, and the A/C didn’t blow cold. But the scrappy Red Line ran like a champ, the turbo issuing a jaunty chirp on upshifts and all 260 horses feeling ready to gallop. It just needed a little deferred maintenance.

I bought some Pirelli P Zeros and got an alignment, since I’ve found that cars drive better with round tires all pointed in the same direction. I changed the oil and recharged the A/C. Next, I tackled the battery, which is mounted somewhere near Earth’s molten core. Accessing it requires removing the right front fender, and I got impatient and only mostly unbolted it, figuring I could bend the flexible composite panel enough to get the battery out. That’s how I tore a fender while replacing the battery, which is not a sequence of words I expected to write back when I told Roger that a Sky Red Line is a discount Viper.

But I stand by my assessment. The Sky was, and is, huge fun. It’s agile and powerful, low-slung and eager to carve a corner. It makes any drive feel like Bowser and Koopa Troopa should be trying to beat you to the finish line of Rainbow Road. The critiques that dogged the Sky when it was new—cheap interior, little storage space, poor visibility—seem less important now. Saturn ran out of time to perfect the Sky, but it’s perfect enough. Dents and all.

Ezra Dyer is a Car and Driver senior editor and columnist. He's now based in North Carolina but still remembers how to turn right. He owns a 2009 GEM e4 and once drove 206 mph. Those facts are mutually exclusive.

#4547. Baby chimpanzees blow ‘raspberries’ because adults do it first

Published Nov 9, 2026 3:00 PM EST

The old adage “monkey see, monkey do,” appears to have a bit of truth to it. Chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes) likely watch adults making different vocalization to learn how and when to use those sounds themselves, particularly when they purse their lips to blow “raspberries.” The findings detailed in a study published today in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) show that the primates’ sounds are not instinctual and set in stone, as previously believed.

Humans learn what words mean from the world around us, and different communities will use different sounds for the same thing. For example, English speakers mimic dogs with “woof,” while French speakers say “ouaf.” When it comes to our primate relatives, biologists generally used to believe that they didn’t learn sounds from one another, and that instead biology dictated their sounds. However, that’s changing with some new research into two groups of Chimpanzees in a couple of west African countries.

To probe how chimpanzees learn to use sounds, the study’s team focused on the raspberry. Chimpanzees make this unvoiced sound that’s similar to how humans push their lips together to blow raspberries. The team looked at how 91 chimpanzees, from birth to 55 years old, used the raspberry call. They studied a group of wild chimpanzees from four communities in Taï National Park, Ivory Coast, and a group of young, orphaned, and peer-raised chimpanzees at Tacugama Chimpanzee Sanctuary in Sierra Leone.

The team found that the wild Ivory Coast chimpanzees almost exclusively used the raspberry while grooming others. However, the juveniles at the Tacugama Chimpanzee Sanctuary used it across a much wider range of social situations.

If blowing a raspberry is only an instinctive call, the groups should be using it in similar ways no matter where they were raised. According to the team, these differences suggest that chimpanzees learn from adults how to make a call, as well as when and why to use it.

“In everyday communication, we use the words that we do only because our peers do too. It’s communal practice that fixes their meaning, rather than features of the words themselves,” Richard Moore, a study co-author and mind, language, and psychology philosopher at the University of Warwick, said in a statement.

“The discovery that this is true not just for natural languages but also some chimpanzee calls means there’s more continuity between chimpanzees’ vocal learning and our own than we previously suspected.”

The team also say that when an adult chimpanzee was introduced to one of the groups living in the Tacugama sanctuary, the young chimps gradually began to use the raspberry more consistently and began to resemble the adult’s noises. This suggests that adults serve as role models, helping a community settle in on shared communication patterns.

The researchers say this is the first time that this kind of learned and agreed-upon sound use has been shown in chimpanzee calls. The link between the raspberry sound and its use appears to be shared from one chimpanzee to another, and is not built in at birth. While chimpanzees struggle to learn entirely new call sounds, the study suggests that they can learn the meaning behind sounds that they already know how to make but didn’t use in the same way as other chimps.

“Even aspects of chimpanzee vocal communication that seemed fixed and unlearned may be shaped by learning, suggesting that there is still much to discover about their vocal repertoire,”

added Antoine Valet, a study co-author and cognitive scientist at the Institute of Cognitive Sciences (CNRS) in France.

Additionally, the team has some theories on why different chimpanzee populations use the raspberry in similar ways if it is a learned sound.

“One possibility is that, whilst grooming, as chimpanzees use their lips to extract parasites from another’s fur, it may be easier to generate a vocalisation that uses similar lip movements, a call that is known to prolong grooming bouts,” explained study co-author and CNRS behavioral ecologist Catherine Crockford. “Communities may have found this useful independently, but that wouldn’t change the fact that the call is a convention. We need more research to test it.”

#4544. Losing even one hour of sleep can make you more susceptible to scams

Published Nov 9, 2026 3:00 PM EST

A poor sleep schedule doesn’t only affect your overall mood, energy levels, and long-term health. New evidence indicates that losing as little as one hour of rest may increase your chance of falling for an online scam by over 10 percent the following morning. Neurobiologists at the University of California, Irvine, laid out their findings in a study published today in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), arguing that even minimal sleep disruptions can have almost immediate consequences.

“Our results demonstrate that even though you may not be aware of it, lack of sleep leads to impulsive choices, and you may lose more than you gain from putting sleep on the back burner,” said UC Irvine neurobiologist and study co-author Eitan Schechtman.

If you have already fallen prey to a scam email in the past, you can at least take some small comfort in the knowledge that you aren’t alone. Cybercrimes continue to increase exponentially in the United States. The FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center received over one million reports in 2025—a nearly 25 percent increase from only five years earlier.

Remaining aware of con artist tactics and staying up-to-date on personal cybersecurity strategies are some of the best ways to protect yourself. However, Schechtman and his colleagues recently wondered if something as seemingly inconsequential as a single evening of bad sleep may also put people at risk for schemes like an email phishing attack. To investigate, the team partnered with a large, unnamed company as it ran a cybersecurity awareness campaign for more than 11,000 employees. Multiple times a year, the company’s IT department issued emails imitating phishing attempts, then tallied how many workers clicked through the fake malicious links. Schechtman’s team then analyzed results both before the switch to Daylight Saving Time (DST), as well as the Monday after employees lost an hour of sleep.

On the Monday prior to DST, workers clicked on a phishing email link about 15.5 percent. of the time. Then, the Monday immediately following DST saw that rate rise to about 17.7 percent. That may not seem like much, but the difference comes out to about a 13 percent increase in phishing victims after losing approximately just one hour of sleep. According to Schechtman, there are multiple ways to contextualize these results.

“First, they give us a peek into the effects of very minor sleep loss… [from] Daylight Saving Time, which is similar in scope to the kind of sleep loss that many of us experience daily,” he said. “Although we focused on cybersecurity, many of our day-to-day decisions are likely compromised in similar ways.”

Schechtman hopes both employers and cybersecurity companies take regularly sleep-depriving events like DST, holidays, and even primetime sporting events into consideration when advising the public on phishing awareness. In the meantime, he stressed that even those who regularly suffer from sleep issues continue to prioritize their rest as much as possible.

“Better sleep likely leads to better decisions,” he added.
